Water evaporation characteristics of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel were recorded and analyzed during drying processes in the moisture analyzer (MX-50, resolution of 0.01%). Figure 5a de- scribes the moisture curves during the drying process at 70, 85, and 100 °C, corresponding to the drying times of 170, 100, and 70 min, respectively. Although the corresponding drying times were different, the curves of cumulative evaporated water had a similar shape and amounted to 1.87 g (93.5% moisture, Figure 5b). The lower drying temperature of 70 °C was suffi- cient to evaporate the hydration layers in the hydrogel. A scien- tific report by Khan et al. demonstrated that the drying of apple tissues at 70 °C is critical to the rupturing of cell membranes, resulting in dehydration of the biological tissues [32]. In the drying process, water at the outer surface evaporated first, fol- lowed by the evaporation of intracellular water. Figure 5c and 5d exhibit the water evaporation rates as a function of drying time and water content in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel. In the first period, the water evaporation rates increased to a plateau of constant drying rate, corresponding to the evaporation of free water molecules at the outer surface [39]. Then, the water evap- oration curves entered into the decreasing rate period where there is deficiency of free water at the outer surface and water transport from the interior to the surface. The critical water content at which the first decreasing rate period began was iden- tified to be about 40% (the left dashed line in Figure 5d). It is noticeable that at the water content of 20% (the middle dashed line in Figure 5d), the water evaporation rates at 70, 85, and 100 °C were approximately half the initial water evaporation rates at 5 min. There is a second decreasing rate period which occurred at the critical water content of 4% (the right dashed line in Figure 5d). Interestingly, in biological tissues, interfacial water integrated in cell walls is also about 2–5% [32]. It is explained that the significantly slower rates of water evap- oration in the decreasing rate period are due to water movement from the interior to the surface and the hydrogen bonding of interfacial hydration layers on the hydrophilic nano- structures. Supramolecular systems with non-covalent interactions and re- versible cross-links are recognized to provide extraordinary properties and applications [45-47]. Reversible self-assembly is an advantage of supramolecular graphene-based hydrogels in comparison with the powder form [13-16]. Hydration layers in between graphene-based sheets not only reduce intersheet binding energy (van der Waals force) but also generate repul- sive forces for exfoliating the macroscopic assembly into nano- scale structures especially under external sonication and me- chanical stimuli. Reversible self-assembly of graphene-based nanosheets in water is essential to many applications, such as adsorption, photocatalysis, biosensing, drug delivery, aqueous paints, and multifunctional coatings [48-50]. Figure 6c exhibits the aqueous dispersions derived from the sonication of GO-SG- ZH hydrogel and powder in water (see Supporting Information File 1, Figure S3). Ultrasound waves vibrated water molecules and created cavitation in the hydrogel structure, leading to the exfoliation of graphene-based nanosheets in water. It is notable that low concentrations (≤50 ppm) are necessary to obtain homogenous dispersions. The ultrasonic dispersion of GO-SG- ZH hydrogels was faster and clearer due to the high content of water intercalation. The GO-SG-ZH powder contained about 10% of water and approximate 60% of nanosilica and zinc hydroxide nanoparticles, which functioned as spacing layers be- tween graphene-based nanosheets. Therefore, the ultrasonic treatment of GO-SG-ZH powder in water also yielded a homo- geneous dispersion. However, the aqueous dispersion of GO-SG-ZH powder was not completely exfoliated in the aqueous environment and quickly settled down. Stacked agglomerates of GO-SG-ZH powder at the bottom of the disper- sion were observed in the micrograph of Figure 6c, while the micrograph of the dispersion of GO-SG-ZH hydrogel showed the absence of stacked structures. Antibacterial properties of graphene oxide–nanosilica–zinc hydroxide in hydrogel and in coating structures The EDS analysis in Table 2 showed that the solid nanocom- posite of GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was composed of 12.81% zinc atoms (derived from the Zn(OH)2 constituent). ZH nanoparti- cles and GO nanosheets in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel are anti- bacterial and antibiofilm agents with low toxicity for food pack- aging and biomedical applications [56,57]. The main antibacte- rial mechanism of GO nanosheets is cell membrane damage caused by direct contact of GO sharp edges with bacterial mem- branes [57,58]. The crucial antibacterial activity of ZH nano- structures is the delivery of Zn2+ ions to disrupt bacterial mem- branes and intracellular processes [59,60]. Antibacterial activi- ty of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was tested in agar well diffusion assays (Figure 9). The photographic results showed inhibition zones against E. coli (Figure 9a) and S. aureus (Figure 9b). The inhibition zones resulted from the diffusion of ZH nanoparti- cles and Zn2+ cations from the hydrogel to the surrounding agar. As the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel is antibacterial, the brush coating of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel on PLA films produced an antibacterial coating on the substrate. Antibacterial tests of uncoated and coated PLA films are de- scribed in Figure 10, where the interfaces between PLA films and agar/E. coli plates are displayed. Before the incubation process, E. coli bacteria did not grow to biofilms (Figure 10a–c). After incubation at 37 °C for 24 h, stripy biofilms of E. coli bacteria were formed on the agar plates (Figure 10d–f). While stripy patterns were observed in the areas of blank PLA film (Figure 10d) and SG/PLA film (Figure 10e), the GO-SG-ZH/PLA film presented an inhibition zone at the vicinity of its boundary (Figure 10f). PLA and SG/PLA were not antibacterial materials, and the GO-SG-ZH coating was effective against the growth of E. coli biofilm on the coating surface. The antibiofilm result is attributed to the antibacterial activities of GO nanosheets and ZH nanoparticles. Regarding the antibacterial mechanism of the nanocomposite coating, direct contact of bacterial cells with sharp nanostructures of the coating is the cause of membrane damage and cell inactivation. 816 Beilstein J. Mechanical properties of polylactide films with nanosilica-based and graphene-based coatings The thin coatings of SG and GO-SG-ZH considerably affected the mechanical properties of plastic films. Tensile testing results of blank PLA, SG/PLA, and GO-SG-ZH/PLA films are de- scribed in Figure 12 and summarized in Table 4. Additional data of measurement values and stress–strain curves are given in Supporting Information File 1, Table S1, Figure S4, Table S2, and Figure S5. Our previous paper presented that GO-ZnO coating on PLA film led to an increase of elastic modulus and a decrease of tensile elongation [14]. Similar trends were also noted in the tensile properties of coated PLA films in this study. Elastic moduli of SG/PLA and GO-SG-ZH/PLA films rose to 2447.08 ± 27.71 MPa and 2232.7 ± 105.52 MPa, which were respectively 31.89% and 20.34% higher than that of blank PLA film. Nanosilica and graphene-based nanosheets were nano- structures with high elastic modulus for reinforcement of PLA films through load transfer mechanism. High elasticity of SG and GO-SG-ZH coatings led to the increases in elastic moduli of the coated films. Besides, considerable decrease of elonga- tion was observed due to the propagation of cracks from the coatings to the substrate. The tensile strength of the GO-SG- ZH/PLA film (54.22 ± 2.86 MPa) was slightly higher than that of the blank PLA film. The enhancement of tensile strength of the GO-SG-ZH/PLA film is explained due to the load transfer from the polylactide substrate to the graphene-based coating during the tensile process. Effective coating adhesion to the substrate and high elastic modulus of graphene-based nano- sheets contributed to the higher tensile properties. While hydration shells participate in the shaping and dynamics of bio- logical structures, water intercalation in graphene-based hydro- gels is proposed to reduce intersheet van der Waals interaction, generate repulsive hydration forces, and facilitate hydration lubrication of graphene-based nanosheets. DFT calculations showed that a water layer in AB bilayer graphene enlarges the intersheet distance from 3.459 to 6.626 Å, and conse- quently leads to a reduction of 37.5% in intersheet binding energy of the van der Waals force. In our experiments, sustain- able green chemistry approaches are used to synthesize graphene oxide, silica gel, nanosilica–zinc hydroxide, and graphene oxide–nanosilica–zinc hydroxide nanocompos- ites. The chemical methods used saved chemical reagents and production energy, converted rice hush ash waste into nanosilica, improved materials quality, and contributed to envi- ronmental sustainability. The GO-SG-ZH hydrogel is a supra- molecular hydration structure with the advantages of aqueous dispersibility, antibacterial activity, and hydration lubrication. Water evaporation analysis suggested that the last 4% of water in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel are interfacial hydration shells on graphene-based nanosheets. The first water shell is crucially re- sponsible for primary hydration forces between nanostructures. Additionally, hydration lubrication is another interesting effect of water-intercalated graphene-based systems. As graphene- based nanosheets in the hydrogel structure are in non-stacking state, they can slide on each other owing to water lubrication and low interfacial friction. After brush coating and water evap- oration, the graphene-based coating is adhered to the polylac- tide substrate through interfacial interactions. The GO-SG-ZH/ PLA films showed antibacterial activity, coating stability, and enhanced tensile properties. In summary, the supramolecular hydration structure of graphene-based hydrogels is a prospec- tive nanotechnology approach to advance nanoscale structures and interfaces for a variety of applications. text: Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10565-025-10064-0 REVIEW Advances in hybrid hydrogel design for biomedical applications: innovations in drug delivery and tissue engineering for gynecological cancers Hua Chang · Heng Wei · Yue Qi · Silu Ding · Hui Li · Si Si Received: 27 March 2025 / Accepted: 22 June 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Hybrid hydrogels have emerged as mul- tifunctional biomaterials for targeted drug delivery and tissue engineering in gynecologic oncology. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the design of hybrid hydrogels that combine polymer net- works with nanomaterials to achieve tunable stimuli- responsiveness, enhanced mechanical strength, and improved biocompatibility. For example, preclini- cal studies of folate‐conjugated liposomal doxoru- bicin have demonstrated enhanced accumulation and antitumor efficacy in ovarian cancer models, while growth factor–loaded hydrogel scaffolds have sup- ported endometrial repair in rodent models. We Hua Chang, Heng Wei, Yue Qi these authors contributed equally to this work. H. Chang · H. Li (*) Department Gynecology, The First Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, Liaoning, China e-mail: yidalihui@163.com H. Wei · Y. Qi Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University, Liaoning, China S. Ding (*) Department of Radiation Oncology, The First Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, China e-mail: dsl1108@hotmail.com S. Si (*) Department of Obstetrics, The First Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, China e-mail: ss_cmu@yeah.net discuss strategies for optimizing drug loading, con- trolling spatiotemporal release profiles in response to tumor‐specific cues (such as pH or enzyme activ- for ity), and customizing scaffold architecture patient‐specific regenerative needs. Implementation challenges—including efficient encapsulation of mul- tiple cargos, precise control over degradation rates, and scale‐up for clinical manufacturing—are criti- cally examined. Finally, we outline future directions, including multifunctional platforms that integrate real‐time monitoring with combined chemo‐immu- notherapy and approaches to address regulatory and translation hurdles. This evidence‐based analysis highlights how hybrid hydrogels can advance preci- sion therapy and regenerative medicine for gyneco- logic cancers while there is a need for further valida- tion in clinical settings. Highlights (1) Hybrid hydrogels integrate poly- mer networks and nanomaterials for tunable, stim- uli-responsive drug delivery in ovarian and cervical cancer. (2) Localized implantation ensures sustained chemo- therapeutic concentration at residual tumor sites, reducing systemic toxicity. (3) Nanoparticle-reinforced scaffolds support pelvic tissue regeneration post-resection while providing immunomodulatory cues. Vol.: (0123456789) 115 Page 2 of 31 Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 (4) Multifunctional platforms combine real-time imaging and chemo-immunotherapy for precision gynecologic oncology. Keywords Hybrid hydrogels · Drug delivery · Tissue engineering · Gynecological cancers Introduction Gynecological cancers are malignant neoplasms of the female reproductive tract, including ovarian, cer- vical, endometrial (uterine), vulvar, and vaginal can- cers. Among these, ovarian and cervical cancers are the most prevalent and pose significant health risks to women worldwide (Hollis 2023; Nebgen et al. 2019). Ovarian cancer, often diagnosed at a late stage due to non-specific symptoms, remains the most lethal gynecological disease(Karnezis et al. 2017). Cervi- cal cancer patients usually contracted persistent high- risk human papillomavirus (HPV), which has seen a decline in incidence due to screening programs and HPV vaccination. However, cervical cancer still rep- resents a major health burden in worldwide low- and middle-income countries (Burd 2003; Sharma et al. 2020). The treatment of gynecological cancers typically involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy (Ferrall et al. 2021; Koh, et al. 2019). Despite advances in these conventional modalities, significant challenges remain. Although surgical resection effectively removes gross tumor masses, it often leaves behind microscopic residual disease that can lead to recurrence (Kahn et al. 2023; Vergote et al. 2011). Chemotherapy, although a cornerstone in the management of advanced-stage cancers, is associated with significant systemic toxicity and the progression of drug resistance (Stein et al. 2021; Konstantinopou- los et al. 2015; Kingnate et al. 2021). Radiotherapy, while targeted, can unintentionally provide collateral damage to adjacent healthy tissues, resulting in per- sistent side effects. Additionally, the heterogeneity of tumors and the unique microenvironment of gyneco- logical cancers further complicate treatment strate- gies, necessitating the progression of more effective and less toxic therapeutic options (Herrera et al. 2019; Dembo 1992; Mayadev et al. 2022). Efficient deliv- ery to gynecologic tumors leverages both passive and active targeting strategies. The enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect allows nanoscale carri- ers to preferentially accumulate in ovarian and uter- ine tumors within the peritoneal cavity due to leaky vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage. Active targeting employs ligands—such as folate, RGD pep- tides, or antibodies against folate receptor α, HER2, or CD44—to promote receptor-mediated endocytosis by cancer cells. Physical guidance methods, includ- ing magnetic field–directed navigation of iron-oxide- embedded hydrogels and focused ultrasound–induced cavitation, further enhance localization to pelvic lesions. Stimuli-responsive triggers (e.g., acidic pH, elevated MMP activity, redox gradients, and hyper- thermia) refine spatial–temporal drug release within the tumor microenvironment. These fundamental mechanisms underpin the subsequent development of hybrid hydrogel vectors tailored for gynecologic oncology applications. However, current approaches fail to bridge the gap between these clinical limitations and precise, local- ized therapy. For instance, residual microscopic dis- ease after surgery can evade systemic chemotherapy, and drug-resistant tumor subclones frequently emerge when drug concentrations fluctuate between sub- therapeutic and toxic levels. Hybrid hydrogels can be engineered to address each of these issues as follows: (1) Residual disease after surgery: Hybrid hydrogels can be implanted or injected into the surgical bed to form an in situ depot that gradually releases chemo- therapeutics or immunomodulators, thereby targeting microscopic foci that might otherwise remain. (2) Sys- temic toxicity and drug resistance: By encapsulating chemotherapeutic agents within a polymeric network, hybrid hydrogels achieve sustained, local drug con- centrations that remain above the resistance-threshold in tumor cells while sparing healthy tissues from high systemic exposure. (3) Collateral damage from radio- therapy: Hydrogels can be loaded with radioprotective nanoparticles or antioxidant compounds that release selectively in peri-tumoral regions, mitigating damage to adjacent normal tissues during and after radiation. (4) Tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental bar- riers: Stimuli-responsive hydrogel matrices can exploit tumor-specific cues (e.g., acidic pH, elevated enzyme activity) to trigger on-demand drug release, overcom- ing barriers such as poor vascularization and hypoxia that limit conventional delivery. At the core of these advances lies the integration of nanotechnology with well-characterized polymer Vol:. (1234567890) Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 Page 3 of 31 115 systems. Specifically, polyethylene glycol (PEG) and chitosan have emerged as leading candidates for gynecologic applications: PEG-based hydrogels are renowned for their excellent biocompatibility, “stealth” properties (minimized protein adsorption), and tunable degradation rates. In ovarian cancer mod- els, PEG hydrogels have been formulated to release cisplatin over several weeks within the peritoneal cavity, maintaining therapeutic drug concentrations while reducing nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression. Chitosan-based hydrogels—derived from deacety- lated chitin—offer intrinsic mucoadhesive and hemo- static properties that are particularly advantageous for cervical and vaginal delivery. When administered intravaginally, chitosan matrices adhere to cervical mucosa and prolong residence time, improving local retention of chemotherapeutics or immunomodulators and enhancing uptake by dysplastic epithelial cells. By combining these polymers with func- tional nanomaterials (e.g., metallic nanoparticles, liposomes, carbon-based nanostructures), hybrid hydrogels can be tailored to the mechanical and bio- logical demands of gynecologic tissues. PEG imparts a hydrophilic, mesh-like network suitable for fluid- rich peritoneal environments, whereas chitosan con- fers mucoadhesion and in situ gelation under mildly acidic vaginal conditions. Such polymer-nanomaterial pairings enable precise control over swelling behav- ior, degradation kinetics, and drug release profiles, thereby addressing the specific clinical shortcom- ings of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy in gynecological oncology. Given the constraints of current therapeutic strate- gies, it is an urgency for innovative approaches that can optimize therapeutic outcomes while lower the risk of adverse effects. Drug delivery systems specifi- cally focus on targeting tumor cells, thereby decreas- ing systemic toxicity, are of paramount importance. Similarly, tissue engineering solutions that can facili- tate the regeneration of tissues damaged by cancer or its treatment are critical for boosting patient sur- vival and life quality (Fig. 1). Figure 1 illustrates four complementary strategies for tumor-targeted nanotherapy. In panel a, lipid vesicles decorated with tumor-specific antibodies engage receptor-mediated endocytosis for active targeting; panel b shows pas- sive accumulation of nanoparticles via the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect in leaky tumor vessels; panel c depicts magnetic guidance of chitosan-coated, 5-fluorouracil-loaded magnetic nan- oparticles under an external magnet to concentrate the drug at the tumor site; and panel d demonstrates focused ultrasound-induced cavitation of circulat- ing microbubbles to transiently disrupt vascular bar- riers (e.g., the BBB), thereby enabling nanoparticle entry—a mechanism that could be adapted to over- come peritoneal or pelvic barriers in gynecologic cancers. Together, these approaches integrate molec- ular recognition, physical forces, and barrier modula- tion to enhance delivery specificity and efficacy, yet each faces critical hurdles—antigen heterogeneity, variable vascular permeability, dosimetry and equip- ment logistics for external fields, and the risk of mechanical tissue damage—underscoring the need for multimodal designs and rigorous preclinical vali- dation. Nanotechnology served as a promising field in this regard, giving novel strategies for both drug delivery and tissue engineering (Ling et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023a). Nanomaterials, due to their small size and large surface area, can be engineered to function in molecular biological systems, helping precise tar- geting and controlled release of drug agents (Cheng et al. 2021; He et al. 2022). Moreover, nanomateri- als can be integrated into scaffold structures for tissue engineering, establishing a conducive matrix for cell proliferation and tissue regeneration(Bharadwaz and Jayasuriya 2020; Li et al. 2017; Tupone, et al. 2021; Grimaudo et al. 2019). For drug delivery, hybrid hydrogels are engi- neered for releasing therapeutic agents in a controlled way when exposed to surrounding stimuli (e.g., pH, temperature, or enzymatic activity). This ensures localized drug release while minimizing systemic exposure (Juthi, et al. 2023; Gao et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2022a; Mauri et al. 2021). This delivery not only enhances the therapy efficacy but also weakens side effects induced by conventional chemotherapy. In tissue engineering, hybrid hydrogels can serve as scaffolds that promote the growth and differentia- tion of cells, aiding the tissue regeneration damaged by cancer or its treatments (Neves et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2017). The integration of nanomaterials within these hydrogels significantly enhances their mechani- cal properties, rendering them ideal for load-bearing applications. Furthermore, nanomaterials can be functionalized with bioactive molecules like pep- tides, extracellular matrix components, or growth factors, which enhance cell adhesion, proliferation, Vol.: (0123456789) 115 Page 4 of 31 Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 Fig. 1 The interaction between nanomaterials and tumor cells. (a) Nanoparticle endocytosis and transcytosis modified by anti- gen–antibody conjugation. (b) Liposomes reach the cancerous area from blood vessels through the EPR effect. (c) Magnetic nanoparticles coated with chitosan carrying 5-Fluorouracil show passive targeting at cancer cells under an external mag- netic field. (d) Therapeutic AuNPs are blocked by the BBB under normal conditions. After FUS exposure, the BBB is tem- porarily opened by microbubble inertial or stable cavitation, allowing AuNPs to pass through. BBB: Blood–Brain Barrier. EPR: Enhanced Permeability and Retention. FUS: Focused Ultrasound and differentiation. This functionalization amplifies the regenerative potential of the hydrogel, facilitat- ing more effective tissue repair and reconstruction in gynecological cancer patients. Additionally, these bioactive molecules can create a conducive micro- environment that mimics natural tissue, encourag- ing more efficient and organized tissue regeneration (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). This is particularly beneficial in restoring the structural modalities and functionality of tissues in the pelvic region, which often bear the brunt of gynecological cancer treatments. As a result, hybrid hydrogels not only give the necessary help for new tissue growth, but also actively enhance the biological processes involved in tissue regeneration, resulting in better clinical outcomes and improved patient recovery. Hybrid hydrogels that combine natural and syn- thetic polymers with nanoscale additives have dem- onstrated remarkable versatility across tissue‐engi- neering and drug‐delivery applications. For cartilage regeneration, porous gelatin methacrylate–poly(2- ethyl-2-oxazoline) scaffolds loaded with kartogenin achieved ≈92% porosity, native‐like stiffness, and sustained chondrogenic induction in vitro (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). Photo-cross-linkable hyaluronic acid bioinks have similarly enabled high‐ fidelity bioprinting of osteochondral constructs, sup- porting cell viability and extracellular matrix deposi- tion under shear forces typical of extrusion processes (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). In repro- ductive‐tissue engineering, polysaccharide‐based hydrogels (e.g., alginate, chitosan, hyaluronic acid) Vol:. (1234567890) Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 Page 5 of 31 115 mimic the endometrial niche, promoting adhesion, proliferation, and controlled release of growth fac- tors—offering new strategies for infertility treat- ment and uterine tissue regeneration (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). Stimuli‐responsive designs further extend these platforms’ functionality by tuning release profiles to local cues. pH-sensitive montmorillonite–PVP/PEG composites released cur- cumin preferentially under acidic, tumor-mimicking conditions and enhanced cytotoxicity in MCF-7 cells compared to free drug (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). Magnetic Fe₂O₃–PEG–agarose nanocomposites regulated 5-fluorouracil delivery via pH triggers, demonstrating biocompatibility and con- trolled release in vitro (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). Together, these studies highlight how judicious selection of polymer–nanomaterial combi- nations and crosslinking methods can meet diverse mechanical, biological, and release‐kinetic require- ments—while underscoring ongoing challenges in standardizing metrics, elucidating long-term in vivo performance, and scaling toward clinical translation. This review highlights the significant progress in hybrid hydrogel design and development for biomedi- cal usage, mainly focusing on drug delivery and tissue engineering in gynecological cancer treatment. By incorporating nanomaterials and advanced hydrogel matrices, these hybrid systems offer enhanced bio- compatibility, mechanical strength, and responsive- ness to stimuli. Their ability to achieve targeted drug delivery reduces side effects and improves therapeutic outcomes, which is critical in reconstructive surgery for gynecological cancers. We emphasize key inno- vations, successful case studies, and future research directions that hold the potential to transform cancer treatment approaches. Hybrid Hydrogels: Composition and Properties Definition and composition Hybrid hydrogels are innovative materials that merge the properties of traditional hydrogels with those of nanomaterials, creating multifunctional systems ideal for advanced biomedical applications (Aliakbarzadeh et al. 2024; Ghorbani et al. 2023; Ghahremani-Nasab et al. 2025). Hybrid hydrogels are three-dimensional, large hydrophilic polymer networks that retain volumes of water while mimicking the extracellular matrix of native tissues. When these networks are integrated with nanoscale components—ranging from inorganic nanoparticles to polymeric and carbon- based nanostructures—the result is a multifunctional platform that combines the swelling and biocompat- ibility of hydrogels with the tailored properties of nanomaterials (Pourmadadi et al. 2024a, 2024b). They are valued for their biocompatibility, flexibility, and ability to be tuned for specific physical proper- ties, rendering them appropriate for drug delivery and tissue engineering (Wang et al. 2021; Cao et al. 2023). The integration of nanomaterials into hydrogels enhances their capabilities. Nanomaterials including nanoparticles, nanofibers, and nanotubes are incor- porated into the hydrogel matrix to impart unique characteristics. These include increased mechanical strength, responsiveness to environmental changes (pH, temperature, or light), and improved drug load- ing and release profiles (Qian et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024). This combination results in a hybrid system where the hydrogel provides a bio- compatible and hydrophilic environment, while the nanomaterials add functionality, making it possible to create versatile platforms for treating gynecological cancers. The increased mechanical strength ensures that the hydrogel can withstand physiological stresses for load-bearing tissues. Responsiveness to environ- mental stimuli permits the targeted release of thera- peutic agents upon encountering specific triggers, ensuring precise drug delivery towards the tumor site. Improved drug loading and release profiles mean that higher doses of therapeutic agents can be incorpo- rated and transferred in a controlled manner, advanc- ing the overall efficacy of the treatment. This hybrid approach achieves the precise targeting and controlled release of drugs, making it a significant advancement in cancer therapy. Furthermore, this method mini- mizes side effects and maximizes therapeutic out- comes, representing a major step forward in the treat- ment of gynecological cancers. These nanoscale additives contribute to hybrid hydrogel performance through two complementary mechanisms: Mechanical reinforcement. Rigid nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene oxide (GO) nanosheets and silica nanoparticles serve pri- marily to bolster the hydrogel’s load-bearing capacity Vol.: (0123456789) 115 Page 6 of 31 Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 and toughness. Multiwalled CNTs, functionalized with –COOH groups to improve dispersion and inter- facial adhesion, can increase tensile strength and fatigue resistance nearly tenfold. Graphene oxide sheets, rich in hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, interca- late within polymer chains to raise the elastic mod- ulus and fracture toughness via hydrogen-bonded networks. Similarly, spherical silica nanoparticles bearing surface silanol (Si–OH) groups form hydro- gen bonds with polymeric backbones, enhancing compressive stiffness and resilience, particularly under cyclic loading. Presentation of biological cues. In parallel, nano- carriers—including liposomes, polymeric nanoparti- cles (e.g., PLGA, PEG–PLGA) and nanogels—offer platforms for precise bioactive signaling. These carriers can be surface-functionalized through car- bodiimide chemistry (–NH₂/–COOH coupling) or thiol–maleimide ligation to present targeting ligands such as RGD peptides, folic acid, or growth factors (e.g., VEGF, FGF), thereby promoting receptor- mediated cell attachment and proliferation. Metallic nanoparticles (gold, iron oxide) further contribute by providing protein-binding surfaces for enzyme immo- bilization or antibody conjugation, enabling com- bined diagnostic imaging and therapeutic (“theranos- tic”) functions within a single hydrogel scaffold. By treating mechanical reinforcement and bio- logical functionality as complementary yet distinct aspects of hydrogel design, this nuanced composition enables the creation of bespoke platforms for targeted drug delivery, tissue engineering and regenerative therapies in gynecological oncology. Types of hybrid hydrogels Interpenetrating networks (IPNs) are a type of hybrid hydrogel comprising two or more polymer networks that are physically entangled but not covalently bonded (Li et al. 2023b). This unique structure allows each polymer network to retain its individual prop- erties while augmenting the overall functionality of the hydrogel. The attributes of improving mechani- cal strength, swelling capacity, and responsiveness to environmental stimuli make them particularly fit for drug delivery and tissue engineering in gynecologi- cal cancer therapy. IPNs provide robust and adaptable scaffolds that support cellular activities and transfer therapeutic agents effectively (Carpentier et al. 2024). In the context of drug delivery, IPNs can accommo- date high drug loads and release them in particular physiological conditions, concerning pH changes within the TME. This release-targeted mechanism guarantees the delivering precision where needed, lessening systemic side effects and boosting treat- ment efficacy. In addition, the enhanced mechanical strength and swelling capacity of IPNs ensure that they reserve their structural integrity, providing con- sistent and reliable performance throughout the treat- ment duration(Wang et al. 2014). For tissue engineering, IPNs offer a versatile plat- form for creating scaffolds that support cell activi- ties. Properties Firstly, hybrid hydrogels are characterized by bio- compatibility, a fundamental property that allows them to engage with biological tissues without elic- iting negative immune reactions. The hydrophilic nature of hydrogels, combined with the inertness of many nanomaterials, promotes cell behaviors(Zhang et al. 2021; Sartore, et al. 2022). It makes hybrid hydrogels ideal for biomedical fields for drug deliv- ery and tissue engineering in gynecological cancers. The biocompatibility of these materials can be fur- ther enhanced by functionalizing them with bioactive molecules or peptides that mimic the extracellular matrix, thereby improving their integration with the surrounding tissue. Secondly, the mechanical strength of hybrid hydro- gels is vital for their application in load-bearing tis- sues and in situations where structural integrity is necessary (Chen et al. 2013). The incorporation of nanomaterials containing carbon nanotubes, gra- phene, or silica nanoparticles significantly enhances the mechanical properties of hydrogels. This results in materials that can withstand mechanical stresses and reserve their shape and functionality in dynamic physiological environments. In the context of gyneco- logical cancer treatment, robust hydrogels can provide durable scaffolds for tissue regeneration, supporting the repair and reconstruction of affected tissues. Thirdly, stimuli-responsive behavior describes how hybrid hydrogels can change physically or chemi- cally when exposed to external stimuli like tempera- ture, pH, light, or magnetic fields (Wu et al. 2010). This property is especially beneficial for targeted drug delivery, enabling precise regulation of thera- peutic agents triggered by external factors. pH-sen- sitive hydrogels can transfer drugs in the acidic con- dition of a tumor, ensuring the targets are delivered directly to tumor cells (Wang, et al. 2020) (Fig. 2). The integration of these stimuli- responsive behaviors into hybrid hydrogels enhances their versatility and effectiveness in drug delivery systems. By incorporating responsive elements, these hydrogels can adapt to the dynamic conditions within the body, providing a smart and adaptable platform for cancer therapy. Characterization of Regular and Stimuli-Respon- sive Hydrogels. A comprehensive suite of physico- chemical and mechanical tests is required to ensure that both conventional and smart hybrid hydrogels meet application‐specific criteria: equilibrium swell- ing studies to quantify swelling ratio and water con- tent; oscillatory rheometry for gelation kinetics and storage/loss moduli; uniaxial compression or tensile tests for Young’s modulus and yield strength; SEM or micro-CT imaging to assess porosity and pore- size distribution; FTIR and NMR analyses to verify chemical composition and crosslink density; DSC and TGA for thermal stability; and Flory–Rehner cal- culations to estimate mesh size. Stimuli-responsive systems further demand dynamic evaluation, includ- ing pH- or temperature-dependent swelling/deswell- ing cycles monitored by rheometry under controlled light- or redox-triggered modulus environments, changes, and in vitro release assays under each trig- ger condition quantified by UV–Vis or HPLC. In situ imaging modalities (environmental SEM or confocal microscopy) can capture real-time network collapse or pore-opening events upon stimulus application (Kulkarni et al. 2023). This multi-modal characteriza- tion framework guarantees reproducible, predictable performance in both standard buffers and biologically relevant microenvironments. In gynecological cancers, this approach can improve treatment survival and lower the side effects caused by chemotherapy. Design and synthesis of hybrid hydrogels Chemical Crosslinking Chemical crosslinking is a critical technique in form- ing hybrid hydrogels, providing them with necessary structural integrity and functionality for biomedi- cal applications, especially in gynecological cancer treatment. This process contains constructing cova- lent bonds between polymer chains to obtain a stable and durable network. Various methods and materials are employed to achieve chemical crosslinking, each contributing unique properties to the final hydrogel. One of the most widely used methods for chemically crosslinking hydrogels is free radical polymeriza- tion (Salahuddin et al. 2021). This technique involves generating free radicals, which initiate the polym- erization of monomers to form polymer chains that subsequently crosslink (Moncada et al. 2023). Free radicals can be generated using thermal initiators, UV light, or chemical initiators. This method is versatile, permitting the addition of diverse functional groups and nanomaterials into the hydrogel matrix. For example, UV-induced free radical polymerization is often employed to create photo-crosslinked hydrogels with precise control over the network structure and mechanical properties(Wang et al. 2023). Additionally, click chemistry represents a highly specific and efficient approach to chemical crosslink- ing. It involves reactions that form covalent bonds between polymer chains with high yield and under mild conditions. A prominent example is the azide- alkyne cycloaddition, which facilitates the formation of robust hydrogel networks(Wang and Zhang 2022; Singh et al. 2022). The specificity and efficiency of click chemistry make it particularly appropriate for biomedical field where precise control over the hydro- gel’s architecture and functionality is required. Enzy- matic crosslinking leverages enzymes to catalyze the formation of covalent bonds between polymer chains. This method is advantageous for its biocompatibility and ability to proceed under physiological conditions. For instance, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) can cata- lyze the crosslinking of phenol-containing polymers within hydrogen peroxide(Chen, et al. 2025; Singh, et al. 2025). Enzymatic crosslinking is particularly useful for creating hydrogels intended for tissue engi- neering and regenerative medicine, where maintain- ing a biological environment is crucial. Physical crosslinking Physical crosslinking is a key method for creating hybrid hydrogels, offering benefits like reduced toxic- ity and the ability to form reversible, stimuli-respon- sive networks. These interactions help form robust yet flexible hydrogels suitable for various biomedical applications, particularly where dynamic and respon- sive properties are needed. Here, we explore various physical crosslinking techniques and their benefits in biomedical fields, especially in drug delivery and tissue engineering for gynecological cancers. One prevalent technique in physical crosslinking is ionic interactions (Sood et al. 2023). This method employs multivalent ions to bridge polymer chains, creating a gel network. It is commonly used with natural poly- mers like alginate, which gels within divalent cations like calcium ions (Ren et al. 2024). The reversible nature of ionic interactions induces the formation of gels that respond to changes in the ionic environ- ment, making them useful for controlled drug release applications. Hydrogen bonding is a key method of physical crosslinking, formed between electronegative atoms and hydrogen atoms. Though weaker than covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds offer enough stability for applications like drug delivery and tissue scaffolding with polymers like PVA and chitosan (Do et al. 2022; Lv et al. 2023). Hydrophobic interactions occur when nonpolar groups in polymers aggregate in water, often used in amphiphilic block copolymers. These interac- tions help form stable hydrogel networks, useful for encapsulating hydrophobic drugs and releasing them in response to environmental changes. like Thermoresponsive gelling uses polymers PNIPAAm that change from soluble to gel at spe- cific temperatures, such as body temperature (Zhang et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2022b). This property ena- bles injectable hydrogels for localized drug deliv- ery and tissue support. Supramolecular chemistry involves non-covalent interactions to form inclusion complexes. This allows for specific and reversible crosslinking, creating hydrogels with adjustable prop- erties ideal for drug delivery and regenerative medi- cine. These techniques provide versatile and effective solutions for various biomedical applications. Physical crosslinking methods offer significant benefits in the development of hybrid hydrogels for biomedical applications. Primarily, these meth- ods reduce toxicity as they do not require harm- ful chemical agents, enhancing the biocompatibil- ity of the hydrogels. Physical crosslinking relies on non-covalent bonds, which allow hydrogels to hand to various stimuli like pH, temperature, and ionic strength(Alexander et al. 2014). This responsive- ness enables controlled drug release and customiza- tion of hydrogel properties, facilitating their high adaptation for specific applications. A major benefit Vol.: (0123456789) 115 Page 14 of 31 Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 of physical crosslinking is the simplicity and prac- ticality of the fabrication process. Unlike chemi- cal crosslinking, which often involves complex and potentially hazardous reagents, physical crosslinking techniques are generally more straightforward. For example, ionic gelation can be easily achieved by mixing a polymer solution with an ionic crosslinker, streamlining the process and making it scalable for larger production(Kono 2014). This simplicity not only reduces the cost and time required for hydrogel synthesis but also improves the reproducibility of the material properties. Furthermore, hydrogels formed through physi- cal crosslinking are often more biocompatible, as they avoid the potential cytotoxicity associated with residual chemical crosslinkers. This increased bio- compatibility is particularly important for biomedical applications, where the hydrogel must interact safely with biological tissues. For instance, in drug delivery systems, physically crosslinked hydrogels can provide a safe and effective medium for controlled transfor- mation of drug agents, reducing the risk of adverse reactions(Yuan et al. 2023). In tissue engineering, the capability of physically crosslinked hydrogels to form networks through non-covalent interactions including hydrogen bonding, ionic interactions, and hydropho- bic interactions allows for the creation of dynamic and flexible scaffolds. These scaffolds can sup- port cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation, promoting tissue regeneration and restoration. The reversible nature of physical crosslinks also means that the hydrogel can adapt to changes in the physi- ological environment, maintaining its functionality over time(Reakasame and Boccaccini 2018). Clinical scalability and regulatory trade-offs: Phys- ical crosslinking techniques—such as ionic gelation, thermo- or pH-induced sol–gel transitions, and supra- molecular host–guest assembly—proceed under mild, catalyst-free conditions, preserving labile therapeutics and obviating cytotoxic residues. This ease of fabrica- tion and compatibility with steam or gamma irradia- tion sterilization makes them particularly attractive for point-of-care vaginal formulations (e.g., chitosan or alginate gels produced aseptically at bedside). However, these non-covalent networks often exhibit lower mechanical integrity and accelerated erosion under high-shear conditions in the peritoneal cavity of ovarian cancer models, resulting in less predict- able drug release. By contrast, chemically crosslinked PEG or genipin-chitosan hydrogels deliver tunable crosslink density, enhanced tensile strength, and pro- longed in vivo residence suitable for both vaginal mucosa and intraperitoneal depots—but necessitate rigorous removal of catalysts or photoinitiators and sterile filtration steps to meet GMP and regulatory requirements. In summary, physical crosslinking methods pro- vide a versatile and effective approach for develop- ing hybrid hydrogels with excellent biocompatibility and responsiveness. By utilizing non-covalent inter- actions containing ionic, hydrogen, and hydrophobic bonds, these hydrogels offer dynamic, reversible, and stimuli-responsive properties that are crucial for drug delivery and tissue engineering applications(Tahir et al. 2025). The simplicity of the fabrication pro- cess, combined with the ability to customize hydro- gel properties, makes physical crosslinking an attrac- tive option for creating safe, efficient, and adaptable hydrogels for biomedical use, particularly in gyneco- logical cancer treatment(Miao et al. 2021). Comparative Evaluation of Crosslinking Strate- gies. Covalent chemical crosslinking methods— such as UV-initiated free-radical polymerization of PEG networks (Ai et al. 2023) or strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) click chemistry in PEG–norbornene hydrogels (Jain et al. 2021)—pro- duce robust covalent bonds that confer high mechani- cal strength (Young’s modulus often > 10 kPa) and sustained, predictable degradation profiles suitable for long-term peritoneal drug depots (e.g., cisplatin release over several weeks) (Shi et al. 2023). How- ever, these approaches typically require potentially cytotoxic photoinitiators or catalysts and thorough post-processing to remove unreacted reagents, which can provoke local inflammation. In contrast, physical crosslinking—exemplified by Ca2⁺-mediated gelation of alginate (Gnanaprakasam Thankam and Muthu 2014) or hydrogen-bonding in PVA–chitosan blends (Gong et al. 2023)—occurs under mild, catalyst-free conditions, enabling injectable, shear-thinning gels ideal for laparoscopic deployment. These non-cova- lent networks avoid toxic residues and grant revers- ible, stimuli-responsive behavior, yet they generally exhibit lower stiffness (< 1–5 kPa) and more rapid erosion under physiological shear, limiting their load- bearing capacity and release precision. Thus, chemi- cal crosslinking is preferred when structural resil- ience and tightly controlled release are paramount, Vol:. These hydrogels form spontaneously from individual molecules into well-defined structures without exter- nal help, triggered by non-covalent interactions like electrostatic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces(Zhao et al. 2019a). This self-assembly is accompanied with unique properties in biomedical fields. Self-assembling hydrogels are created by design- ing molecular building blocks that interact to form a 3D network. These blocks include peptides, poly- mers, and small molecules. Peptide-based hydrogels use amino acids that develop structures of alpha- helices or beta-sheets through hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, which then aggregate into stable hydrogel networks(Gnanaprakasam Thankam and Muthu 2014). Polymer-based self-assembling hydrogels often use amphiphilic block copolymers, composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments. In an aqueous environment, the hydrophobic seg- ments aggregate to minimize water exposure, lead- ing to micelle formation and further organization into a hydrogel. Additionally, electrostatic interactions play a role, with charged polymers forming networks through attraction or repulsion(Gong et al. 2023). Self-assembling hydrogels offer significant advan- tages in drug delivery because thsy can encapsulate and release therapeutic agents based on a controlled mode. Their porous structure allows for incorporating diverse drugs, such as small molecules, nucleic acids and proteins (Chou and Tsai 2021). For gynecological cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can target tumor site with chemotherapy, lessening systemic side effects and increasing the effectiveness. These hydro- gels can be injected in a minimally invasive manner, further increasing their clinical appeal(Han et al. 2009). In tissue engineering, self-assembling hydrogels are highly promising because they are biocompatible, have adjustable mechanical properties, and can imitate the extracellular matrix. They provide ideal scaffolds for supporting cell growth and tissue regeneration. By incorporating bioactive molecules such as growth fac- tors, peptides, and extracellular matrix components, these hydrogels can promote specific cellular behaviors like adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation (Zhao et al. 2019a; Ashraful Alam et al. 2013). For gyneco- logical cancers, self-assembling hydrogels can aid in reconstructive surgery following tumor resection. They offer a temporary matrix that supports tissue regen- eration and gradually degrades as new tissue forms. Additionally, these hydrogels can release drug agents to combat residual tumor cells, reducing the risk of recurrence. Preclinical validation in dynamic pelvic environ- ments: Recent studies have begun to translate self- assembling hydrogels into orthotopic gynecological cancer models. In a murine orthotopic ovarian cancer model, an injectable thermosensitive self-assembling polyplex–hydrogel formulation achieved sustained intraperitoneal retention, reducing tumor burden by 62% compared to free polyplexes and preserving mechanical integrity under peritoneal fluid shear for over seven days (Zhao et al. 2019a; Ashraful Alam et al. 2013). Similarly, a supramolecular peptide amphi- phile hydrogel loaded with triptolide, when adminis- tered intraperitoneally in nude mice, demonstrated a 55% reduction in ascites volume and maintained more than 50% of its initial storage modulus after repeated peritoneal contractions (Zhao et al. 2019a; Ashraful Alam et al. 2013). Moreover, urea-modphile hydrogels exhibit enhanced stability and rapid self-healing under cyclic compressive strains, retaining over 80% of their initial storage modulus after three compression cycles (Zhao et al. 2019a; Ashraful Alam et al. 2013). These in vivo data confirm that self-assembling systems can withstand the stresses of the pelvic cavity while provid- ing localized, sustained drug release. Overall, self-assembling hydrogels denotes a sig- nificant advancement in biomedical fields, providing innovative solutions for drug delivery and tissue engi- neering in treating gynecological cancer. Their ability to develop functional and versatile structures is a prom- ising option for improving patient survival and innovat- ing cancer therapy. Applications in gynecological cancer drug delivery Targeted drug delivery systems The design of targeted drug delivery systems focus on enhancing the precision and efficacy of cancer treatment by directing therapeutic agents specifically to tumor tissues. The mechanisms of action in these systems typically contain the use of nanomaterials to carry and transfer drugs within a control(Luo et al. 2023). These nanomaterials are engineered to spot and bind to specific molecular markers expressed on tumor cells. It guarantees that the drug payload is concentrated in the tumor microenvironment. One common mechanism refers to the usage of ligand- receptor interactions. Ligands, like antibodies, pep- tides, or small molecules, are bind to the surface of nanocarriers(Hennink and Nostrum 2002). These ligands specifically interact with overexpressed recep- tors on the surface of cancer cells. For example, in gynecological cancers, overexpressed folate receptors are observed on the surface of OV cells. Nanocarriers conjugated with folic acid can technically target these cells, facilitating the localized delivery of chemo- therapeutic agents (Dodda et al. 2021; Hu et al. 2022; Porfiryeva et al. 2024). Another mechanism used is the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, which takes advantage of the unique properties of tumor blood vessels(Cuenot et al. 2022). Tumors have leaky vessels and poor lymphatic drainage, allowing nanoparticles to accumulate more effectively in tumor tissue than in normal tissue. This passive targeting is commonly used for nanoparticle-based drug deliv- ery. Furthermore, stimuli-responsive drug delivery systems release drugs in response to specific tumor microenvironment triggers, such as pH, tempera- ture, or enzyme activity. For example, pH-sensitive Vol:. (1234567890) Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 Page 17 of 31 115 hydrogels release drugs in the acidic environment of a tumor, ensuring precise delivery (Han et al. 2020). Targeted drug delivery systems offer several signif- icant advantages over traditional chemotherapy. The primary benefit is the reduction in systemic toxicity. Traditional chemotherapy involves the administration of drugs that circulate throughout the body, affecting both cancerous and healthy cells. This non-specific action leads to serious side effects, including hair loss, nausea, and immunosuppression (Lu and Wang 2018). In contrast, targeted delivery systems concen- trate the drugs at the tumor site, thereby reducing col- lateral harm on normal tissues. Another advantage is the improved efficacy of the treatment. By delivering more drugs directly to the tumor, these systems can enhance the therapeutic impact while using lower overall doses of the drug. It not only maximizes the drug’s efficacy but also mitigates the adverse effects caused by high-dose chemotherapy (Zhu et al. 2024; Li et al. 2019). Gynecologic‐specific outcomes and implications: In the randomized, open‐label phase III MIRASOL trial (NCT04209855), 453 patients with folate recep- tor α–positive, platinum‐resistant ovarian cancer received mirvetuximab soravtansine or investiga- tor’s‐choice chemotherapy; mirvetuximab signifi- cantly extended median progression‐free survival to 5.62 months (95% CI, 4.34–5.95) versus 3.98 months (95% CI, 2.86–4.47; HR 0.65; P < 0.0001) and median overall survival to 16.46 months (95% CI, 14.46–24.57) versus 12.75 months (95% CI, 10.91–14.36; HR 0.67; P = 0.0046), while reducing rates of grade ≥ 3 adverse events (41.7% vs. 54.1%) and discontinuations due to toxicity (9.2% vs. 15.9%) (Zhu et al. 2024; Li et al. 2019). Likewise, a retro- spective cohort of 69 women with recurrent epithe- lial ovarian carcinoma treated with extended‐dura- tion single‐agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (median 11 cycles, cumulative dose 400 mg/m2) reported a median PFS of 13.0 months (95% CI, 10.7–15.2) and median OS of 40.2 months (95% CI, 30.0–49.0), with a 59.4% clinical‐benefit rate (com- plete response 17.4%, partial response 13.0%, sta- ble disease 29.0%) and acceptable grade ≥ 3 derma- tologic toxicity (31.9%) (Zhu et al. 2024; Li et al. 2019). These gynecologic‐specific data demonstrate that ligand‐targeted and EPR‐based nanocarriers can deliver both survival gains and improved tolerability in ovarian cancer. Moving forward, optimizing patient selection via FRα expression, refining dosing sched- ules, and incorporating predictive biomarkers will be crucial to maximize therapeutic index and broaden application to other gynecologic malignancies. Additionally, targeted drug delivery systems can overcome multidrug resistance (MDR) in treating cancer. MDR often results from the overexpression of efflux pumps in cancer cells that expel therapeu- tic agents, reducing their effectiveness (Xing et al. 2022a). Nanocarriers can bypass these efflux pumps, ensuring that the drug remains inside the cancer cells long enough to exert its therapeutic effect. The ver- satility of nanomaterials used in targeted drug deliv- ery also allows for the combination of diagnostic and therapeutic functions. These technologies support simultaneous imaging and therapy of tumors, provid- ing instant feedback on the treatment’s progress and allowing for adjustments as needed. Case studies and clinical trials The application of targeted drug delivery systems using hybrid hydrogels and nanomaterials has shown promising results in the treatment of gynecological cancers. One notable example is the use of folate- conjugated liposomal doxorubicin for ovarian cancer treatment (French et al. 2016; Casadidio et al. 2025; Zhao et al. 2019b). In this approach, doxorubicin, a potent chemotherapeutic agent, is encapsulated in liposomes conjugated with folic acid (Xing et al. 2022b). This allows the drug to specifically target ovarian cancer cells overexpressing folate receptors. Clinical studies have demonstrated that this targeted delivery significantly reduces the systemic toxic- ity commonly associated with doxorubicin, while enhancing its efficacy against ovarian tumors (Liu, et al. 2022; Lima-Sousa et al. 2023). Another suc- cessful application involves the use of poly (lactic- co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles loaded with paclitaxel for cervical cancer (Ak et al. 2018; Zou et al. 2012). PLGA nanoparticles provide a sustained and controlled release of paclitaxel, which is crucial for maintaining therapeutic drug levels at the tumor site. Clinical trials have shown that patients receiv- ing paclitaxel-loaded PLGA nanoparticles experience fewer side effects and improved tumor regression compared to those receiving traditional paclitaxel treatment (Corbin et al. 2013; Hu et al. 2025; Braet et al. 2023). The design of scaffolds needs to think about sev- eral factors, such as porosity, biodegradability, mechanical strength, and biocompatibility. Poros- ity is a core indicator that influences nutrient diffu- sion, cell infiltration, and waste removal within the scaffold (Wang et al. 2022). Biodegradability is another key aspect of scaffold design. The scaf- fold’s degradation rate should align with the pace of new tissue formation, ensuring a gradual load trans- fer to the new tissue without structural failure. Bio- degradable polymers, such as PGA, PLA, and their copolymers, are commonly used in scaffold fabrica- tion for their predictable degradation profiles and biocompatibility(Lawrie, et al. 2013b). Mechanical strength is crucial for scaffolds designed for load-bearing applications, making sure they can tolerate physiological forces without suc- cumbing to collapse or deformation. This is particu- larly important in gynecological contexts, such as the pelvic floor, which is subjected to significant mechan- ical stress. Incorporating nanomaterials like carbon nanotubes or graphene can enhance the mechanical properties of scaffolds, providing additional support while maintaining necessary flexibility(Liu, et al. 2021). Biocompatibility is equally essential, ensur- ing the scaffold does not trigger an adverse immune response when implanted(Xu et al. 2020a). Materi- als used in scaffold construction should be neither be toxic nor provoke an immune reaction, and promote cellular activities. Regenerative medicine The usage of hybrid hydrogels in regenerative medicine is particularly beneficial for gynecological applications. For instance, in patients undergoing surgery for ovar- ian or cervical cancer, there is often a need to repair or reconstruct tissues that have been removed or dam- aged (Hamoudeh et al. 2008). Hybrid hydrogels can be designed to degrade at a controlled rate, allowing them to provide temporary support until the newly regener- ated tissue is strong enough to function independently. This degradability is achieved by selecting appropri- ate biodegradable polymers PLGA and tuning their degradation kinetics to match the tissue regeneration rate (Zhou et al. 2022; Ramezani Farani et al. 2022). Moreover, hybrid hydrogels can be functionalized with bioactive molecules. These bioactive agents are critical for enhancing the regenerative potential of the hydro- gels by promoting cellular activities. For example, the incorporation of VEGF into the hydrogel can stimulate angiogenesis, providing the newly forming tissue with a blood supply necessary for its survival and function (Nigam and Bahadur 2017; Hao et al. 2020). For clinical translation, hybrid hydrogels have been engineered for minimally invasive implanta- tion and predictable in vivo clearance. They can be delivered through standard 5–12 mm laparoscopic trocars as shear-thinning precursor solutions that rap- idly gel in situ under physiological or light-triggered crosslinking, without requiring specialized instru- ments (Nigam and Bahadur 2017; Hao et al. 2020). Upon implantation, the hydrogel network supports host cell infiltration and neovascularization, while controlled enzymatic degradation aligns scaffold resorption with new tissue formation over 4–6 weeks. Importantly, incorporating sequential immunomodu- latory cues—such as pro-inflammatory solvents that drive early M1 polarization followed by anti-inflam- matory moieties that induce M2 polarization—pro- motes efficient clearance of hydrogel remnants by macrophages and minimizes fibrotic encapsulation (Nigam and Bahadur 2017; Hao et al. 2020). These materials are ideal for post-surgical repair due to their capacity to degrade at controlled rates, provide temporary struc- tural support, and facilitate tissue regeneration. By incorporating bioactive molecules, these hydrogels can enhance cellular responses and tissue healing, promoting the regeneration of critical tissues dam- aged by cancer surgery. Their versatility and adapta- bility position hybrid hydrogels as a powerful tool for improving patient outcomes in gynecological cancer treatment and beyond. Clinical applications The use of hybrid hydrogels in treating gynecologi- cal cancer has shown great results in clinical settings. For example, a PEG-based hydrogel loaded with doxorubicin has been tested for ovarian cancer. Clini- cal trials demonstrated tumor reduction with fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy(Sabbatini et al. 2008). The biocompatibility and controlled drug release properties of the hydrogel provided a sus- tained therapeutic effect, improving patient outcomes. This highlights the potential of hybrid hydrogels as an effective and safer alternative in cancer treatment. Another successful application involves the use of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels incorporating cispl- atin for cervical cancer (Kotcherlakota et al. 2017). Clinical trials have indicated that these hydrogels pro- vide localized, sustained release of cisplatin, resulting in improved tumor regression rates and reduced sys- temic toxicity. The use of hyaluronic acid, showing its natural biocompatibility to interact with cancer cell receptors, has been instrumental in the success of this treatment approach. Recent advancements have also seen the integra- tion of immunotherapy with hybrid hydrogels. For example, a clinical study utilized chitosan-based hydrogels combined with checkpoint inhibitors for treating endometrial cancer (Wang et al. 2020). The hydrogel matrix facilitated the localized delivery of immune modulators, boosting the immune response against cancer cells and demonstrating significant improvements in patient survival rates. Thus, hybrid hydrogels have shown great potential in clinical applications for treating gynecological cancer, giv- ing more effective, localized, and safer alternatives to conventional therapies. Their ability to provide controlled drug release, reduce systemic toxicity, and enhance immune responses underscores their promis- ing role in improving patient outcomes and advancing cancer care. Translational Challenges and Clinical Consid- erations: Bringing hybrid hydrogels from bench to bedside entails navigating complex regulatory path- ways for combination drug–device products, often requiring both an Investigational New Drug (IND) application and an Investigational Device Exemp- tion (IDE), as well as compliance with pharmaceuti- cal (e.g., 21 CFR 210/211) and medical-device (21 CFR 820) GMP standards. Achieving batch con- sistency and scalability demands tight control over polymer molecular-weight distributions, nanoma- terial dispersion, and crosslink density—necessi- tating validated in-process analytics and stringent quality acceptance criteria for each production run. Rigorous safety assessment protocols, aligned with ISO 10993 biocompatibility testing and GLP toxi- cology studies, must evaluate both acute and chronic responses, including local inflammation, degradation by-products, and systemic exposure associated with long-term implantation. Encouragingly, early-phase clinical trials are now underway: phase I/II studies of thermosensitive poloxamer hydrogels delivering paclitaxel in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and of hyaluronic acid–cisplatin depots in recurrent cervical carcinoma, have reported acceptable local tolerability and sustained intratumoral retention, though final effi- cacy data are pending. Addressing these regulatory, manufacturing, and safety hurdles will be essential to realize the full clinical potential of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology. Challenges and future directions Current limitations Biologically, the integration of hybrid hydrogels within the human body poses challenges related to biocompatibility and immune response. While these materials are designed to be biocompatible, individ- ual variations in patient responses can lead to unpre- dictable outcomes. For instance, some patients may experience inflammatory reactions or fibrosis at the site of hydrogel implantation, which can compromise Vol.: (0123456789) 115 Page 24 of 31 Cell Biol Toxicol (2025) 41:115 the therapeutic efficacy of the treatment(Bhandari et al. 2022). Moreover, the degradation rates of bio- degradable hydrogels need to be precisely matched with tissue regeneration rates to avoid premature loss of structural support or prolonged presence of for- eign materials, which could lead to chronic inflam- mation. For immunocompromised gynecologic cancer patients—particularly those recently treated with cytotoxic chemotherapy—may exhibit impaired monocyte/macrophage clearance and dysregulated complement activation upon exposure to nanopar- ticle–polymer composites. This can result in pro- longed hydrogel retention, low-grade inflammation, or hypersensitivity reactions. To mitigate these risks, surface modifications such as PEGylation or zwitteri- onic coatings are recommended to minimize protein- corona formation; the use of endogenous polymers (e.g., hyaluronic acid or chitosan) can leverage “self” signals to reduce immune recognition; and incorpo- ration of enzyme-degradable linkers (e.g., MMP- cleavable peptides) or low-immunogenic crosslink- ers (e.g., genipin) helps ensure controlled clearance without overt activation of host defenses. We further recommend preclinical immunotoxicity screening in chemotherapy-conditioned murine models and in vitro assays using patient-derived PBMCs to fully characterize immune interactions prior to clinical translation. Despite notable advances, several critical chal- lenges hinder the reliable translation of hybrid hydro- gels for gynecologic applications. First, reproducibil- ity in hydrogel synthesis remains problematic: minor variations in polymer molecular weight, crosslinking kinetics, or mixing conditions can yield markedly dif- ferent network architectures and mechanical proper- ties. Second, batch-to-batch variability—driven by inconsistencies in raw-material purity, crosslinker concentration, and processing parameters—often leads to unpredictable drug-loading efficiencies and degradation profiles. Third, sterilization protocols pose a dilemma: common methods such as gamma irradiation, autoclaving, or ethylene-oxide treatment can induce polymer chain scission or alter crosslink density, compromising scaffold integrity and thera- peutic payload stability. Finally, in vivo degradation frequently diverges from in vitro expectations due to heterogeneous enzyme activity, localized pH shifts, and variable immune cell infiltration within the pel- vic cavity, resulting in inconsistent scaffold resorption and drug-release kinetics. Rigorous process control, standardized quality metrics, validated sterilization methods, and more predictive animal models will be essential to overcoming these hurdles and ensuring reproducible clinical performance. Remaining Gaps and Controversies: Despite remarkable progress in designing and preclinically validating hybrid hydrogels for gynecologic oncol- ogy, key gaps and debates persist. First, the mecha- nistic interplay between specific nanomaterials (e.g., graphene oxide, PLGA nanoparticles) and the com- plex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, with conflicting reports on how hydrogel stiffness and degradation by-products influence ovarian ver- sus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, and rheological properties hinders direct comparison across platforms and laboratories. Third, immuno- genicity remains controversial: although genipin- crosslinked chitosan matrices have been reported to elicit minimal inflammation, other studies document macrophage activation and fibrotic encapsulation with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli- responsive trigger (pH, enzyme, thermal, or light) is still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is strik- ing—only a handful of formulations have entered early‐phase clinical trials, underscoring challenges in scaling, sterilization, regulatory compliance, and long-term safety. Addressing these controversies through rigorous mechanistic studies, harmonized testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts will be vital to accelerate the clinical translation of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care. Innovations on the horizon Emerging technologies and materials offer potential solutions to these challenges. One such innovation is developing smart hydrogels which can respond to multiple stimuli, such as pH, temperature, and enzy- matic activity. They can provide more controlled and localized drug release, enhancing the precision of cancer treatments(Yu et al. 2022). Advanced nano- including carbon-based nanostructures materials, (graphene and carbon nanotubes) and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), are being explored for their exceptional mechanical properties and functional Vol:.
