Although no acute toxicity was observed, our additional chronic toxicity experiments indicated that continuous and repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L induced significant mortality over time. LT50 values of FSNPs from our study were similar to those previously reported for A. salina, where LT50 values of 18.8 and 17.9 days were observed following exposure to SNPs at concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/L, respectively30. Two possible mechanisms may account for this delayed toxicity. First, while FSNPs could be excreted from the digestive tract, continuous exposure resulted in their persistent presence in the gut, potentially causing blockage that impaired food digestion and assimilation, ultimately leading to starvation11. Second, toxic effects of FSNPs as discussed earlier may emerge with repeated or prolonged exposure19,22. This could explain the significant increase in mortality observed in the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups after 6 days, despite the absence of detectable accumulation following depuration. Although this study demonstrated the effects of FSNP exposure on brine shrimp through behavioral and survival assessments, it did not include biochemical or molecular biomarkers, which could provide deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms of toxicity. Previous studies have shown that exposure to NPs can alter enzymatic activities related to oxidative stress and detoxification pathways in Artemia, including glutathione S-transferase (GST), catalase (CAT), and cholinesterase (ChE)38,39. For example, Gambardella et al.39 reported that metal oxide NPs significantly altered GST and ChE activities, even in the absence of acute mortality, highlighting their importance in xenobiotic metabolism and neurotoxicity assessment. Similarly, Varó et al.38 found that amino-modified polystyrene NPs induced oxidative stress and modulated gene expression related to development (clap), molting (cstb), stress response (hsp70), and immunity (proPO and lysozyme) in A. franciscana. Additionally, transcriptomic analyses have shown that exposure to SNPs can affect genes involved in stress response and cuticle renewal in aquatic invertebrates40. These findings suggest that prolonged FSNP exposure may plausibly affect cellular and molecular pathways in Artemia, even in the absence of apparent acute toxicity. Therefore, future studies incorporating gene expression and enzymatic biomarkers would be valuable for confirming the mechanistic basis of FSNP-induced stress and toxicity. Conclusions This study demonstrated that FSNPs present a promising tool for observing the feeding behavior of marine zooplankton. They showed excellent dispersion stability in seawater and exhibited low acute toxicity. Critically, they were effectively ingested and expelled by the brine shrimp, allowing for a clear observation of the feeding processes without adhering to the shrimp’s outer surfaces or causing significant adverse effects. Our findings indicate that FSNPs can be utilized to track the passage of ingested food through the gut, providing valuable insights into the feeding behavior of zooplankton. FSNPs at 16 mg/L were sufficient to mark the shrimp without affecting their locomotion during short time exposure. However, prolonged or repeated exposure negatively affected survival, indicating potential long-term risks. The presence of food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs from their digestive tract. Their ease of observation under UV light makes them particularly useful for such Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:25897 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-11858-2 10 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ applications. Future research should investigate the molecular-level effects of FSNPs on zooplankton and assess their bioaccumulation and biomagnification potential in other marine species to evaluate their broader applicability in ecological studies. Materials and methods Nanoparticle characterization FSNPs were synthesized according to the method outlined by Songvorawit, et al.15 using the water-in-oil reverse microemulsion technique, and Rubpy dye (tris [2,2′-bipyridyl]ruthenium[II] chloride) as a fluorophore. The NPs were examined under a JEM-1400 transmission electron microscope (TEM; JEOL, Tokyo, Japan), and their size was measured from the TEM images employing the ImageJ software version 1.53o (NIH, USA; https://imagej.nih.gov/ij). Since this study used FSNPs suspended in saline water, their dispersion stability was examined in artificial seawater (ASTM D1141-98, pH 8.2) utilizing a Nano ZSP zeta-sizer (Malvern Panalytical, Great Malvern, England). Emission spectra were examined employing a Duetta™ fluorometer (Horiba Scientific, Kyoto, Japan) at excitation bands of 365 and 460 nm, which corresponded to the UV light wavelength used to track animal behavior in this study and the maximal excitation wavelength of Rubpy dye, respectively14. The maximal emission wavelength of the FSNPs was calculated using a moving average based on five data points. Test animals and handling Commercial brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana) cysts (American Eagle, USA) imported from the Great Salt Lake, USA were purchased from a local supplier in Bangkok, Thailand. They were hatched in artificial seawater at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and illumination. For rearing adult shrimp, nauplii (shrimp larvae) were transferred into an 8 L tank and raised in filtered natural seawater (3% salinity) at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) under a 12/12 h illumination cycle. Artificial food (composition unknown, branded as N.P. Guppy, Thailand) purchased from a local seller in Bangkok, Thailand, was provided every other day, and the adults were obtained 3 weeks after hatching. Euthanasia was performed utilizing the two-step method (immersion in 5% ethanol for 5 min and then 10% formalin) per the AVMA guidelines41. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University (Protocol Review No. 2423018). Acute toxicity test Nauplii, 18–24 h post-hatching, were transferred into 24-well plates containing 1–1,024 mg/L of FSNP suspension in artificial seawater (2 mL of suspension and 10–20 nauplii per well) and cultured at 25–26 °C under a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) with a 12/12 h light/dark cycle. Brine shrimp grown in artificial seawater without FSNPs were used as a control. Mortality and immobility were checked at 24 and 48 h after exposure. A nauplius was considered dead if its appendages stopped moving within 10 s. Immobility was identified when a nauplius remained with moving appendages in situ for 10 s and was calculated by dividing the number of immobile (but still alive) individuals by the total number of living individuals. A mortality rate in the 24-h period of less than 10% was considered valid for the control group. Each treatment was conducted in eight replications. Test for the appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking To ensure that all tested brine shrimp were ready to eat the food provided, 15–30 nauplii, 24–36 h after hatching were used. They were incubated in 2 mL of FSNP suspension in 24-well plates for 1 h at 25–26 °C in the dark under two conditions: food presence (1 × 106 cells/mL of baker’s yeast) or food absence. They were then euthanized. The fluorescence due to FSNP intake, which was visible through the body wall, was inspected under a stereo microscope coupled with a UV lamp set to 365 nm. To minimize observer bias, the same examiner conducted all observations throughout the experiment. The fluorescence brightness was scored on a scale ranging from 0 to 2: 0 = no, 1 = slight, and 2 = bright fluorescence (Fig. 2). The marking efficiency was calculated following the formula described previously15,42, as shown in Eq. (1): M arking ef f iciency (%)= 100 (nb × (B ∑ × b) × Nb) (1) where nb is the number of brine shrimp with each score value, b is the brightness score, B is the highest possible score (here: 2), and Nb is the total number of scored brine shrimp. However, some brine shrimp possibly did not exhibit feeding behavior during the testing period, resulting in no fluorescence (score 0) and a low marking efficiency. Therefore, further analysis based on the fluorescence brightness of the marked individuals (score 1 or 2 only) was calculated by applying Eq. (2): F luorescence brightness score(%) = 100 N 2 (N 1+N 2) × (2) where N1 is the number of brine shrimp with a fluorescence brightness score of 1 and N2 is the number of brine shrimp with a fluorescence brightness score of 2. Every treatment was conducted in five replications. Effects on locomotion Nauplii, 18–24 h old after hatching (n = 46), were incubated in 24-well plates containing 16 mg/L FSNP suspended in artificial seawater (0.5 mL of suspension and 1 nauplius/well) at 25–26 °C under a 12/12 h light/dark cycle for 24 h. The locomotion of each individual was recorded for 30 s using a TG-4 digital camera (Olympus, Tokyo, Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:25897 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-11858-2 11 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ Japan) at a frame rate of 30 fps. The traveled distance and average speed were analyzed employing AnimalTA version 2.3.4, an animal tracking software43. Nauplii in artificial seawater without FSNPs were used as a control (n = 42). Effects on the feeding rate Nauplii, 18–24 h after hatching, were transferred into glass vials (50 nauplii per vial) containing 10 mL of a suspension mixture of dead baker’s yeast (~ 2 × 105 cells/mL, heat-killed at 70 °C for 5 min) with or without 16 mg/L FSNPs. The vials were dark incubated at 25–26 °C. A 0.1 mL aliquot was taken from each vial at the beginning and after incubation for 12 h to count the number of yeast cells on a hemacytometer. A suspension of yeast without FSNPs and nauplii was utilized as a control to estimate the rate of yeast autolysis. The feeding rate was calculated by following Li, et al.3, as shown in Eq. (3): Feeding rate = 100 × C0 (t − × Ct N ) (3) where C0 and Ct are the density of yeast (cells/mL) at the beginning and end of the experiment, respectively, t is the incubation period (h), and N is the number of brine shrimp in the vial. Each treatment was conducted in seven replications. Persistence of FSNPs in brine shrimp A depuration experiment was conducted under food presence or absence. Baker’s yeast powder was used as food. Nauplii, 18–24 h after hatching, were dark-incubated in a suspension mixture of 16 mg/L FSNPs and 1 × 106 cells/mL of baker’s yeast for 1 h. Then, the nauplii were washed with seawater and passed through a 110 μm net. Next, 5–10 nauplii were transferred into each well of a 24-well plate containing 2 mL of seawater and 1 × 106 cells/mL baker’s yeast. After euthanasia, the fluorescence of FSNPs consumed by the nauplii was observed under a stereo microscope equipped with a UV lamp and an Axioscope 5 fluorescence microscope (ZEISS, Oberkochen, Germany) at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 min, as well as 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h. The number of nauplii with observable FSNPs was counted irrespective of the fluorescence brightness. Under food absence, the entire experiment was conducted with the same procedure, but without yeast. Each treatment was conducted in eight replications. To examine whether FSNPs moved along with the ingested food, another experiment similar to the depuration described above was conducted by providing brine shrimp nauplii with DAPI-stained baker’s yeast as food and FSNPs simultaneously. The nauplii were then examined under a fluorescence microscope. Chronic toxicity test Based on the results of the appropriate FSNP concentration experiment, a concentration of 16 mg/L FSNPs was used for the chronic toxicity test. Brine shrimp nauplii (18–24 h post-hatching) were transferred to 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 150 mL of artificial seawater under continuous aeration, with 10 nauplii per flask. They were fed with artificial food, and both seawater and food were renewed every 48 h. Three treatment groups were performed: (1) continuous exposure to FSNPs, (2) 3-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h, and (3) 6-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h. In treatments (2) and (3), nauplii were exposed to FSNPs prior to the renewal of seawater and food. The experiment was conducted over a period of 14 days. A control group was maintained in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Rearing conditions and mortality assessment criteria were consistent with those used in the acute toxicity test. Each treatment was conducted in nine replications. Test with adult brine shrimp Adult brine shrimp, 25 males and 24 females, were used to evaluate whether FSNPs could be applied to developed stages. The sexes were determined by the presence of a clasping organ (male) and brood sac (female). The shrimp were randomly selected from an aquarium and transferred into 24-well plates filled with 2 mL of baker’s yeast suspension (1 × 106 cells/mL), one individual per well. They were dark-acclimatized for 30 min. The FSNP suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs. Statistical analyses Because our data did not meet the assumption for parametric statistics, nonparametric statistical analyses were used in all tests. The effects of FSNP concentration on mortality and immobility were ascertained by applying the Kruskal–Wallis test; Dunn’s test was used for pairwise comparison. The effects of FSNP concentration, the presence or absence of food, and their interaction with the marking efficiency or fluorescence brightness of the marked individuals were analyzed employing the aligned rank test. Feeding rates in the presence and absence of FSNPs were corrected for the rate of yeast autolysis in the control group and then compared by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The effects of depuration time, the presence or absence of food, and their interactions were analyzed using the aligned rank and Dunn’s tests. Locomotion data for shrimp treated with FSNPs were compared with the control utilizing the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The number of times that the abdomen of adult brine shrimp exhibited luminescence and the number of times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of FSNPs were compared between sexes using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. LT50 was analyzed using probit analysis in SPSS version 28.044. All other statistical analyses were performed using the base, ARTool, combinate, dplyr, survival, survminer, and tidyverse packages in R, version 4.3.045. Pacheco-Salazar *a Nowadays, the use of self-cleaning surfaces is increasing globally, especially after the COVID-2019 pandemic, and the use of nanoparticles has been shown as a plausible option for this purpose. In the present study, Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystals were successfully synthesized (in the copper content range of 0–30 mol%) using the polymeric precursor method. The structural, morphological, vibrational, and antibacterial activity were carefully studied to unveil the eﬀect of copper ions on the properties of the hosting matrix, aiming at maximizing the usage of Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystals. The results show fabrication of nanoparticles near their respective exciton Bohr diameter (5.4 nm for SnO2), however, monophasic SnO2 was observed up to 15 mol%. Above this limit, a secondary CuO phase was observed, as shown by the assessed X-ray diﬀraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared, and Raman spectroscopy data. Furthermore, the redshift of the primary A1g vibrational mode of SnO2 is successfully described using the phonon-conﬁnement model, demonstrating a good relationship between the Raman correlation length (L) and the crystallite size (hDi), the latter determined from XRD. Regarding the antibacterial activity, assessed via the disc-diﬀusion testing method (DDTM) while challenging two bacterial species (S. aureus and E. coli), our results suggest a rapid diﬀusion of the nanoparticles out of the paper disc, with a synergistic eﬀect credited to the Sn1−xCuxO2–CuO phases contributing to the inhibition of the bacteria growth. Moreover, the DDTM data scales with cell viability, the latter analyzed Received 27th July 2023 Accepted 18th September 2023 DOI: 10.1039/d3ra05089k rsc.li/rsc-advances using the Hill equation, from which both lethal dose 50 (LD50) and benchmark dose (BMD) were extracted. 1 Introduction Nowadays, inorganic antimicrobial agents such as semi- conductor oxide nanostructures (TiO2, ZnO, CuO, and SnO2) are promising for cleaning surfaces because they are non-toxic, have a high surface-to-volume ratio, visible transparence and have higher thermal stability than organic antimicrobials,1 which makes it feasible to cover objects like tables, doorknobs, and tactile mobiles to produce self-cleaning antimicrobial surfaces. Besides, SnO2 nanocrystals with small physical dimensions, particularly those around the exciton Bohr diam- eter,2 exhibit drastically diﬀerent properties from their bulk counterparts. The bottom-up method based on chemical synthesis routes of nanocrystals is one method to produce aUniversidad Nacional de San Agust´ın de Arequipa, Arequipa, Peru. Among the methods used to produce SnO2 nanocrystals, one can list the hydrothermal,3 co-precipitation,5 and polymeric precursor methods. Furthermore, aer reaching a certain size, nanocrystals can be further engineered by doping, as this seems to be independent of the type of dopant used and the synthesis method.6–8 Although doping is a highly eﬀective method for manipulating magnetic, electrical, and optical properties of oxide semiconductors, it is an extremely complex process, leading to end properties that are strongly inuenced by the position of the dopant ion within the crystal lattice, the nal oxidized state, and ionic radii. By doping oxide semiconductors, such as transition metal- doped SnO2 (TM-SnO2) or earth rare-doped SnO2 nano- particles, one targets a wide range of applications, including the use of self-cleaning surfaces (SCS). In this regard, one can mention the use of doped SnO2 nanoparticles, which recently gained attention due to antibacterial activity. Studies have shown that these nanoparticles can inhibit the growth of various bacterial species, including Gram-positive and Gram- negative bacteria,9,10 given that doping enhances antibacterial activity; the highest values reported in the literature are also 28482 | RSC Adv., 2023, 13, 28482–28492 © 2023 The Author(s). These nd- ings have been described in several studies, where doping metals such as Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Ce have been used, and the maximum diameter inhibition zone (DIZ) value has been found of for nanoparticles.9,11–13 In this regard, the report of Sathishkumar et al. can be highlighted, displaying and increase in antibacte- rial activity (using a 10 mm disc) as the doping content and concentration of Cu-doped SnO2NPs (30, 40, 50, and 60 mg −1) increase, leading to the highest DIZ values of 18 and mL 19 mm for the S. aureus and P. aeruginosa bacteria, respectively, while using a sample of 9 mol% Cu-doped SnO2 and 60 mg −1 concentration.9 However, the exact mechanism by which mL doping enhances the antibacterial activity of TM-SnO2 nano- particles is not fully understood, although it is believed that the presence of transition metal ions can extend carrier recombi- nation by the increase of defect centers, acting as trapping cores. This can lead to an increase in the generation of super- −2, which is the precursor of other oxide (cO reactive oxygen species (ROS), being responsible for the anti- bacterial eﬀect of TM-SnO2 nanoparticles.14 ROS have a strong ability to oxidize a wide range of organic-based materials, such as pollutants, bacteria, cancer cells, and viruses. When doped oxide semiconductors are used as self-cleaning surfaces, the ROS generated on the surface can cause oxidative stress in bacterial cells, destroying cell walls, DNA, and relevant proteins.6 The research of new materials with SCS activity is of extreme importance, especially aer the COVID-2019 pandemic. In this scenario, we can highlight the use of Cu-doped oxide semiconductor with high antibacterial activity while it is irra- diated with UV light.15 However, UV light is not feasible for creating self-cleaning and antibacterial surfaces in typical indoor conditions, with negligible UV light exposition. There- fore, it is necessary to search for alternatives aiming at to increase antimicrobial response in a dimly illuminated envi- ronment. Also, no previous investigation has been carried out to evaluate the inuence of doping enrichment of the surface and the onset of a secondary phase on the antibacterial activity of the system, indicating a knowledge gap. −/ cO In this study, we aim to investigate the synthesis and char- acterization of Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles, with emphasis on structural, morphological, and vibrational properties plus antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli (ATCC® 33876) and Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC® 25923) in a dark environment. We also explore the possible mechanisms by which Cu-doping contributes to enhance the antibacterial activity of the as- synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles. Our ndings are expected to contribute to the development of novel materials for self- cleaning surfaces with high antibacterial activity. 2 Experimental details Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystals were synthesized using the poly- meric precursor method (Pechine's method), using tin chloride monohydrate hexahydrate (Cu(NO3)3$6H2O), ethylene glycol (C2H4(OH)2) and citric acid (SnCl2$H2O), copper nitrate (C6H8O7)as reactive chemicals. More details about the used synthesis protocol have been described in the literature.16 X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) measurements were performed using a Rigaku MiniFlex 600 X-ray diﬀractometer equipped with Cu Ka radiation (l = 1.5418 Å) and scanning in the 2q range of 20– 80°. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were obtained using a Zeiss microscope, model EVO10, and JEOL Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) model JSM 7001F, where X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) is implemented to deter- mine the chemical composition of the samples. Transmission images were obtained using electron microscopy (TEM) a Talos™ F200i commercial microscope. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements were carried out (samples pressed in KBr pellet) using a Bruker VERTEX 70 FT-IR spectrometer, scanning in the wavenumber range of 450– −1. Room temperature Raman spectra were recorded 4000 cm using a Horiba Labram HR Evolution spectrometer equipped with the 532 nm laser line. The agar disc-diﬀusion testing method (DDTM) was used to evaluate the inhibition zone (IZ) associated with the S. aureus and E. coli species. The DDTM is made up of a xed amount (5 mg) of Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystal impregnated on lter paper discs (6 mm of diameter), which are placed on the surface of a Petri dish culture medium (Mueller– Hinton agar) containing the appropriate bacterium (S. aureus or E. coli). Aer placing the paper discs, the Petri dish was placed in an incubation chamber kept at 35 °C for 24 and 48 hours for E. coli and S. aureus, respectively, with the in vitro tests per- formed in triplicate (×3). 3 Results and discussions XRD patterns of undoped and Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles are shown in Fig. 1(a). The main crystalline phase is linked with the rutile tetragonal unit cell SnO2 phase, as indicated by the main peaks found at 26.5°, 33.8°, 37.9° and 51.7° associated with the (110), (101), (200) and (211) plane reections, respectively. However, additional peaks at 35.5° and 38.7° were observed in copper concentrations starting from 20%, which have been respectively linked with the (111) and (022) planes of the secondary CuO phase; the latter suggesting that the solution limit is lower than 20 mol%, this being due to the detection limit of the technique. To determine the structural parameters the XRD patterns were analyzed using Rietveld renement implemented in EXPGUI, a graphical user interface for GSAS soware,8 where a Lorentzian peak shape (S) was used to model the diﬀraction peaks proles, S = X/cos q + Y tan q, with the rst term repre- senting the Lorentzian Scherrer whereas the second term describes the strain broadening. A typical t is shown in Fig. 1(b), where the open black circles are the recorded experi- mental data, the solid red line is the theoretical curve, and the solid green line at the bottom is the diﬀerence between them. Table 1 displays the structural parameters extracted from the Rietveld renement. The lattice constants for the undoped SnO2 nanoparticles are a = b = 4.7339 Å and c = 3.1894 Å, giving a unit cell volume of 71.374 Å3. It is worth noting that above this range (7.5– 15 mol%), the Raman shi is unaﬀected because excess of Cu- ions are converted into the CuO secondary phase. title: Cu-doped SnO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticles: size and antibacterial activity investigations.
authors: Aragón FFH, Villegas-Lelovsky L, Castillo-Llanos JI
Solis JL, Peralta-Alarcón GH, Pacheco-Salazar DG

text: www.nature.com/scientificreports Fabrication of biodegradable nanocomposite scaffolds with hydroxyapatite, magnetic clay, and graphene oxide for bone tissue engineering Akram Babakhani1, Seyed Jamaleddin Peighambardoust1, Maryam Ghahremani-Nasab2,4 & Naeimeh Sadat Peighambardoust3 Bone tissue engineering offers an alternative approach to producing scaffolds using biodegradable materials. The extracellular matrix of bone tissue comprises collagen and hydroxyapatite so that regenerated scaffolds can be a combination of polymeric materials and hydroxyapatite. Additives are also used to improve the properties and bring the properties of the regenerated scaffold closer to bone tissue. This study focuses on developing nanocomposite scaffolds composed of natural polymers carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and alginate (Alg), combined with the synthetic polymer polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as the polymer matrix. The mechanical properties of these biopolymers were enhanced using magnetic clay nanoparticles modified with graphene oxide (CGF) and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp). Modified clay was synthesized by adding graphene oxide (via the modified Hummer’s method), clay, and Fe3O4 nanoparticles. Nanocomposite scaffolds were prepared using the freeze- drying process, incorporating 10 wt. % HAp and 2 wt. % CGF as optimal additives. Comprehensive characterization, including XRD, FT-IR, TGA, SEM, and analysis of porosity, swelling, degradation, and biomineralization, confirmed the formation of a porous polymer matrix with favorable properties. The optimal PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF scaffold demonstrated compressive strength of 12 MPa, porosity of 72%, swelling of 1860%, and biodegradation of 43% over 21 days, while the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffold exhibited a compressive strength of 8.1 MPa and porosity of 79%. Both scaffolds showed good biomineralization in SBF and a favorable cell viability rate (OD) in MTT toxicity tests, with an OD of 1.483 and 1.451 for PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffolds, respectively. These findings suggest that the PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold is a promising candidate for bone tissue engineering applications. By adding hydroxyapatite and magnetic clay modified with graphene oxide to the polymer scaffold, the mechanical properties of the scaffold are increased, appropriate porosity and swelling values are obtained, and desirable cell viability is achieved. Keywords Magnetic nanoclay, Hydroxyapatite, Nanocomposite scaffold, Graphene oxide, Bone tissue engineering Failure of tissues and organs due to damage, congenital disabilities, and aging is becoming the main issue of human body health all over the world. Bones are one of the strongest and primary tissues of the body, maintaining the surrounding soft tissues1. Regarding synthetic scaffolds that promote bone tissue repair, the dual role of bone tissue engineering (BTE) scaffolds in interacting with the extracellular matrix and providing load-bearing capacity is a challenge. This research aims to investigate the use and processing of several materials and hierarchical architectures to simulate the structure of natural bone tissues so that they may function as bioactive artificial scaffolds2. It is widely believed that designing and preparing new tissues is one of the most 1Faculty of Chemical and Petroleum Engineering, University of Tabriz, Tabriz 5166616471, Iran. 2Stem Cell and Regenerative Medicine Innovation Center, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran. 3Koç University Boron and Advanced Materials Application and Research Center (KUBAM), 34450 Sariyer, Istanbul, Turkey. 4Department of Tissue Engineering, Faculty of Advanced Medical Sciences, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran. email: j.peighambardoust@tabrizu.ac.ir Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:22235 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-07270-5 1 OPEN www.nature.com/scientificreports/ effective and efficient ways that tissue engineering can accelerate bone regeneration during the healing process3. A new strategy for repairing bones has emerged that is based on tissue engineering. As a result of its use of biomaterial scaffolds along with cells and growth factors, it can induce the formation of new bone tissues while reducing the risks associated with autologous bone grafts4. Bone tissue is a composite of approximately 70% nano-hydroxyapatite and 30% collagen. Wet collagen and the accumulation of mineral crystals penetrate each other and form a mineral fiber on a scale of several hundred nanometers. The primary role of bone is to provide a structural framework and mechanical strength, regulate blood pH, and maintain calcium and phosphate levels for metabolic processes5. It is desirable to design a biocompatible composite that can mimic the natural extracellular bone matrix and accelerate new bone regeneration6. If the dispersed phase used in the composite is nanoparticles, the composite material will be a nanocomposite. Natural bone is an example of a nanocomposite composed of two major phases, organic and inorganic, at the nanoscale7. Polymer-based nanocomposites are attractive due to their ability to create porous architectures and biodegradability. The ease of manipulating structures with precise tuning of physicochemical properties is an advantage of polymer nanocomposites for tissue engineering applications such as dental, bone, and neural engineering8. Nanocomposites made of polymeric materials and additives are potential materials for constructing bone scaffolds9. Polymers for making hydrogels include natural and synthetic polymers. Natural polymers are mainly natural components that prepare scaffolds with high biocompatibility, biodegradability, and natural cell adhesion. Recently, synthetic polymers have been widely used to make bone tissue engineering scaffolds because they have high mechanical properties and long life. Carboxymethyl cellulose is a biocompatible and biodegradable anionic polymer that can create a strong ionic cross-link in the scaffold10 and increase the biochemical characteristics of porosity, swelling, and degradation. Cellulose is mainly used for various biomedical applications11. Among natural polysaccharides, alginate biopolymer is also widely used as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering. Alginate is one of the most well-known substances, and it has the property of forming a suitable scaffold that can be useful for the treatment of organ failure and loss. Alginate consists of guluronic acid and mannuronic acid and is used in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, abundance, and low price12. Alginate hydrogels can increase minimal protein absorption due to their hydrophilic property13. Sodium alginate is anionic and can be dissolved in water. Hydroxyl groups can cause strong interactions between sodium alginate and other polymers through hydrogen bonding14. Alginate benefits osteoblast growth due to its functional groups, such as hydroxyl and carboxyl, and increases the efficiency of implant substrates. Due to its high degradation rate in cell culture, its use in biomedical applications is limited. To improve alginate’s biocompatibility and mechanical properties, its combination with synthetic polymers and clay minerals was investigated15. Given the disadvantages of natural polymers, such as poor solubility in common solvents, their low mechanical properties, and poor stability in physiological environments, There have been numerous studies conducted on the physicochemical properties of composite polymers, which have proven to be effective in overcoming the disadvantages of natural polymers16. Blending polymers is a potential method for improving mechanical flexibility17. Polyvinyl alcohol is a hydrophilic semi-crystalline synthetic biopolymer containing many hydroxyl groups, and it can also form hydrogen bonds with free water molecules18. Polyvinyl alcohol is biocompatible and has high mechanical strength, low toxicity, large surface area, and good chemical stability; in a clinical setting, its use is possible to construct membranes, repair tissues, and construct biomaterials16. By synergistically combining the bioactive properties of nanoparticles and the properties of polymers, composite materials create scaffolds that provide an optimal environment for cell proliferation, differentiation, and cell adhesion19. Various natural and synthetic fillers are used as strengthening agents to improve polymer scaffolds’ mechanical properties and bioactivity. Clay is considered one of the mineral fillers that will enhance the biological and mechanical properties of the scaffold significantly, and it has already been studied in bone cement processing20. Clay can be essential in bone regeneration and repair, increasing osteoblast differentiation and apatite deposition20. Also, the graphene oxide filler is highly compatible with the polymer matrix due to the attendance of polar groups on the surface of this material. The high exceptional area ratio and antibacterial properties make GO a promising material for developing bone tissue’s antimicrobial and antiviral surface21. GO is exfoliated from graphite and contains epoxide, carboxylic, and carbonyl ketone groups in its structural plane. Graphene and graphene-based materials have been investigated in various fields, such as bioimaging, biosensors, cancer treatment, drug delivery, and tissue engineering. Unique properties such as thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, high surface area, ease of operation, flexibility, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity make it suitable for biological applications. GO has osteoconductive and osteoinductive ability to regulate osteoblast differentiation22,23. Also, this substance can force stem cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation even without adding a growth factor24. Hydroxyapatite contains basic elements such as calcium and phosphate, essential for bone growth. HAp particles increase cell proliferation and adhesion and improve bone tissue conduction23. Hydroxyapatite has unique properties, such as excellent biocompatibility and low toxicity25. Combining ceramic filler and polymer matrix in one material produces composites with polymer plasticity and calcium phosphate bioactivity26. Scaffolds containing HAp have stronger mechanical properties and higher cell proliferation than scaffolds containing TCP, which gives them a better function in bone regeneration in the early stages27. Nanoparticle content can be used to modify the properties of polymer nanocomposites28. Various magnetic nanoparticles have been developed recently for use in biological applications. Among these nanoparticles, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe3O4) have biocompatibility and good performance for medical applications. Many researchers have shown that the magnetic properties of Fe3O4 nanoparticles make it an ideal material for cell isolation and drug delivery, which also increases the effect of bone induction. Several studies have shown that integrating Fe3O4 nanoparticles with polymer fibers solves the compaction problem and improves their stability in biological applications29. The research fabricates nanocomposite scaffolds using CMC, Alg, PVA, magnetic clay nanoparticles modified with graphene oxide (CGF), and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) to enhance mechanical properties. Characterization involved XRD, FT-IR, TGA, and SEM analyses, assessing porosity, swelling, degradation, and biomineralization, and the MTT Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:22235 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-07270-5 2 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ test evaluated cell viability. In bone tissue research, the composites studied mainly combine a natural and synthetic polymer and an additive, each of which can only be used to improve one property. In this study, two biopolymers are compared in terms of the composition of scaffolds. Two additives are also used: HAp can be used to improve biomineralization, and CGF is a combination of several materials that can give many favorable properties to the polymer composite for use as a polymer scaffold. Having the required mechanical properties is one of the most important properties that bone tissue replacement scaffolds must possess. In addition to having the required mechanical properties, the scaffolds should possess other characteristics required by bone tissue, such as porosity, biocompatibility, swelling, and non-toxicity. A significant aspect of the research is that in addition to increasing compressive strength, attention has been paid to maintaining the required porosity of the bone tissue. A combination of graphene oxide, clay, hydroxyapatite, and the magnetic material Fe3O4 has been used in this research as a new material. As a result of the combination of graphene oxide with clay, the compressive strength of the scaffold was increased significantly, and the presence of HAp led to an increase in biomineralization of the scaffold, whereas Fe3O4 had a positive effect on the viability of the cells. The properties of natural bone differ significantly based on its type. For example, the compressive strength of cancellous bone ranges from 2 to 20 MPa. As a result, it is important to consider the scaffold’s mechanical properties when designing scaffolds for bone reconstruction and fracture healing to ensure a successful outcome30. It has been found that the scaffold that was prepared in this study has compressive strength within the acceptable range for cancellous bone. It is important to emphasize that the porosity of a hydrogel is a significant factor that profoundly affects the fate of bone cells31. A series of interconnected pores in this hydrogel facilitate the migration of cells, the permeability of nutrients, the removal of waste materials, and the penetration of blood vessels and nerves32. The porosity of cancellous bone ranges from 30 to 70%33. The porosity of the scaffolds prepared for this study is within an appropriate range for cancellous bone scaffolds. The prepared scaffolds had appropriate degradation rates because replacing the manufactured tissue with the original tissue would have to occur within a proper biodegradation range. Also, they exhibited a high degree of cell viability. Materials and methods Materials Sodium alginate (Na-Alg) polymer with a molecular weight of 12,000–40,000 Da from Sigma Aldrich, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose with a molecular weight of 70,000 g/mol and a deacetylation degree of 90% from Samchun, Korea, and polyvinyl alcohol with a molecular weight of 72,000 g/mol and a hydrolysis degree of 95% from Merck were used in this study. Potassium hydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), and 25% glutaraldehyde as cross-linkers were obtained from Merck. The acids used in this study, including hydrochloric acid (HCl) 37%, phosphoric acid (H3PO4), acetic acid (CH3COOH) 100%, and sulfuric acid (H2SO4) 98%, were all obtained from Merck. Cloisite 30B clay was organically modified to be the clay used in the study, obtained from Southern Clay Company. K2HPO4.3H2O, KCl, NaCl, Na2SO4, MgCl2.6H2O, NaHCO3, CaCl2.2H2O, and TRIS salts prepared simulated body fluid purchased from Merck. Iron (II) chloride, Iron (III) chloride, KMnO4, and H2O2 were used to modify clay. Synthesis of graphene oxide To prepare graphene oxide using the modified Hummer method. First, 3 g of graphite powder was added to the H2SO4/H3PO4 mixture (40:360 ml), and then 18 g of KMnO4 was added and stirred at 50 °C for 14 h with 100 rpm by a magnetic stirrer. The temperature of the resulting mixture was reduced to 25 °C, and then 30% H2O2 was added to it, making the mixture light brown and stirred for 20 min. A centrifuge was used to separate the mixture, and several washes were done with distilled water to reach a neutral pH. In a vacuum oven, 24 h of drying time was spent at 70 °C on the synthesized graphene oxide34. Graphene oxide was synthesized in black and in powder form. Preparation of magnetically modified clay To prepare magnetically modified clay, 1 g of synthesized graphene oxide (GO) was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 35 min, while 2 g of Cloisite 30B clay was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 20 min. A solution of iron(III) chloride and iron(II) chloride in a 1:2 molar ratio was then added to the GO-clay mixture, which was heated and stirred at 90 °C for 20 min. The resulting mixture was gradually combined with a 4 M sodium hydroxide solution and stirred for 50 min. Finally, the modified clay was separated from the solution, washed several times with distilled water, and baked at 105 °C for 4 h. Preparation of natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) powder The chicken femur was cleaned entirely of meat and remaining materials to prepare natural hydroxyapatite powder and then boiled for 45 min in boiling water. The cleaned bones were placed in a furnace for 3 h at 900 °C with a nitrogen atmosphere. After the set time, the bones are removed from the oven, cooled to room temperature, and then powdered once they are at room temperature. The production efficiency of natural hydroxyapatite powder is 58%, and the product is white35. Preparation of nanocomposite scaffold The nanocomposite scaffolds were prepared using natural polymer materials, PVA, hydroxyapatite extracted from natural bone, and modified clay using a simple mixing method. For the preparation of the scaffold, a solution of 2 wt. in the first step. % of a natural polymer in distilled water was prepared by dissolving the polymer in the water and stirring the solution until the polymer was fully dissolved. As soon as the materials had been prepared, they were added in the correct proportions, and the mixer was turned on for 12 h. 0.5 v/v % of glutaraldehyde was added to the prepped solution in 5% of the total solution volume to cross-link the polymer solution. Mechanical properties study The mechanical properties of the scaffold samples were evaluated by measuring the compressive strength prepared by freeze-drying. To assess the material’s compressive strength, cylinder samples measuring 12 mm in height and 6 mm in diameter were cut. During a compression test, a force with 0.5 mm per minute speed and power of 25 kN was used to test the material’s compressive strength at 25 °C. A universal machine model was used to carry out mechanical tests, Al-7000-Taiwand. Three samples of each scaffold were prepared to perform the compressive strength test, and all three samples were tested. Their average compressive strength was reported as the compressive strength of the polymer scaffold. The error value was 0.1 MPa. Measuring the porosity of scaffolds Using the liquid displacement method, we could determine the porosity of scaffolds36. Scaffolds were cut into one cubic cm square piece. A displacement liquid was employed in this case, and it was ethanol because it does not dissolve the scaffolds while it is being used. To determine the porosity of the cut scaffolds, the scaffolds were placed in a graduated container containing ethanol with volume (V1) to measure the porosity. Using the total volume of ethanol and scaffold (V2), we calculated the volume difference V2-V1. After exiting the scaffold from the cylinder containing ethanol, the remaining volume of the ethanol in the cylinder was measured by using the following formula: V3. According to the equation below, the scaffold porosity could be estimated using the following equation: ε = (V1 − (V2 − V2) V3) (1) Swelling test of scaffolds Initially, the cut scaffolds were weighed (Winitial) and then immersed in PBS phosphate buffer solution for 24 h for incubation. After incubation, the samples were removed from the buffer solution, and any excess water was blotted off with filter paper. The swelling test was repeated three times for each sample. The swelling ratio for each sample was calculated using the following equation37: Swelling Ratio = (Wﬁnal − Winitial) Winitial (2) Biodegradation test of scaffolds Scaffolds were given the exact dimensions and weighed. Then, the scaffold samples were incubated in a phosphate buffer solution for 21, 14, and 7 days at 37 °C with pH = 7.4. After the specified time, the samples were dried using the freeze-drying method and weighed. The scaffold destruction rate was obtained by the following equation37: Biodegradation Ratio = (Initial weight of sample Weight of sample in time T) − Initial weight of sample (3) Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) study The thermal stability of the polymer raw materials and nanocomposite scaffolds was assessed using TGA. A thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA-PL, TGA 1500, Canada) was employed for this analysis, conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere within the 25–600°C temperature range. Investigation of scaffold biomineralization using simulated body fluid (SBF) The performance of the scaffold bone graft was assessed using simulated body fluid (SBF), which was prepared following established protocols with chemical reagents. SBF is essential for examining the formation of biomaterials on polymer scaffolds. To prepare the solution, 1000 mL of SBF was made by adding 700 mL of deionized water into a plastic container in a water bath. It is recommended to cover the container with either a glass or plastic lid while stirring; for the process to be successful, the solution should be kept at a consistent temperature of 36.5 °C throughout. Adding the ingredients in order is essential; once each ingredient is dissolved completely, the next one should be added, and so on. As soon as the ingredients were added, hydrochloric acid was used in the amount of 0–5 ml with an additive solution to achieve a pH of 7.4 in the resulting solution after adding the ingredients. A total of 1000 mL of solution was prepared by adding water to a flask and shaking it at 20 °C to reach the desired volume. The solution was then transferred to a polyethylene container and stored in a refrigerator at 5–10 °C. Scaffold samples were immersed in the SBF solution and incubated at 37 °C for 14 days. After incubation, the samples were removed, rinsed with distilled water, and dried using the freeze-drying method. Finally, EDX and SEM techniques were employed to evaluate the biomineralization capability of the scaffold samples38. Assessment of toxicity and cell viability First, uniform pieces of scaffolds were cut and immersed in 70% ethanol solution for 30 min to sterilize them. Eventually, we must continue using PBS to remove any remaining ethanol from the system and transfer it to a 96-well cell culture plate. Then, mesenchymal stem cells were cultured on the scaffolds with a cell density of 1 × 104 cells per cell plate. They were incubated for 72 h at 37 °C. After 72 h, the supernatant of all the wells of the 96-well plate was removed, and after washing with PBS to each well, 0.2 ml of MTT solution (5 mg/mm) was added, and the wells were kept in the incubator for four hours. It was incubated at 37 °C. A solution of 0.1 mL DMSO was then substituted for the MTT solution for 30 min. Finally, the absorbance was measured by an ELISA reader at a wavelength of 570 nm to determine cell viability. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analysis The morphological properties of HAp obtained from the femur of chicken, modified clay, and synthesized scaffolds have been evaluated using FESEM analysis and EDX analysis. As seen in Fig. 3a, the produced HAp has a crystalline structure. In Fig. 3b, as seen in the EDX analysis of HAp, the elements Mg, Na, and Zn are observed in addition to the main elements P and Ca. text: OPEN Sb2Te3 nanoparticle‑containing single‑walled carbon nanotube films coated with Sb2Te3 electrodeposited layers for thermoelectric applications Rikuo Eguchi , Koki Hoshino & Masayuki Takashiri * Single‑walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are promising thermoelectric materials owing to their flexibility and excellent durability when exposed to heat and chemicals. Thus, they are expected to be used in power supplies for various sensors. However, their thermoelectric performances are inferior to those of inorganic thermoelectric materials. To improve the thermoelectric performance while maintaining the excellent characteristics of SWCNTs, a novel approach to form inorganic thermoelectric layers on the SWCNT bundle surfaces using electrodeposition is proposed. We synthesized Sb2Te3 nanoparticle‑containing SWCNT films and coated them with electrodeposited Sb2Te3 layers. The Sb2Te3 nanoparticles were synthesized via a spontaneous redox reaction, which were then added to a SWCNT dispersion solution, and films were produced via vacuum filtration. At higher nanoparticle contents in the films, the Sb2Te3 electrodeposited layers completely covered the SWCNT bundles owing to the increase in the concentration of precursor ions near the SWCNT bundle surface, which in turn was the result of melted nanoparticles. The thermoelectric performance improved, and the maximum power factor at approximately 25 °C was 59.5 µW/(m K2), which was 4.7 times higher than that of the normal SWCNT film. These findings provide valuable insights for designing and fabricating high‑performance flexible thermoelectric materials. Thermoelectric generators are promising energy harvesting devices. They produce electrical energy via carrier diffusion in response to heat flux produced by a temperature gradient in thermoelectric materials. The widespread development of Internet of Things (IoT) has facilitated the emergence of the flexible thermoelectric generator technology1–4. This is because the IoT technology requires a large number of sensors, and wireless power supplies for the sensors using ambient heat sources are indispensable for the technology. In addition, the flexibility favors the installation of generators in a variety of heat sources, such as human bodies and curved surface objects5–8. Generally, flexible thermoelectric materials include conductive organic materials9–11, single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs)12–14, and their composites15–17. Among them, SWCNTs are excellent as power supplies for IoT sensors because they exhibit excellent heat and chemical durability. Although SWCNTs demonstrate excellent characteristics for flexible thermoelectric generators, their thermoelectric performances are inferior to those of inorganic chalcogenides such as Bi2Te3-based alloys18. The thermoelectric performance is expressed by the dimensionless figure-of-merit ZT = σS2T/κ and power factor PF = σS2, where σ, S, T, and κ represent the electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, absolute temperature, and thermal conductivity, respectively. To increase the thermoelectric performance, an effective approach is to combine the SWCNTs with inorganic thermoelectric materials. Jin et al. used a sputtering technique to fabricate a flexible thermoelectric material comprising highly ordered bismuth telluride (Bi2Te3) nanocrystals anchored on a single-walled carbon nanotube network; this material exhibited a high Seebeck coefficient19. Wu et al.20 prepared hybrid thin films of p-type SWCNTs and antimony telluride (Sb2Te3) nanoplates, which exhibited high power factors, through the combina- tion of vacuum filtration and annealing. In addition to these studies, excellent thermoelectric materials have been proposed by combining CNTs with inorganic and organic compounds21,22. These pioneering studies motivate us to further increase the thermoelectric performance by combining the SWCNTs and inorganic chalcogenides. A favorable approach is to coat the SWCNT bundle surface with an inorganic chalcogenide via electrodeposition26–28. As electrodeposition is a wet process, not only the surface of the SWCNT film but also the inside of film can be electrodeposited by the electrolyte penetrating the gaps in the film. However, it is challenging to effectively deposit the inorganic layer on the SWCNT bundle surface29. This is because the SWCNT films in the bundle form exhibited low electrical conductivity compared to metals30–32, and several precursor ions in the electrolyte were not attracted to the SWCNT bundle surface. Therefore, it is necessary to explore different methods for performing electrodeposition on the SWCNT bundle surface33. In this study, a novel approach was performed to increase the thermoelectric performance of the flexible SWCNT films. We mixed Sb2Te3 nanoparticles with an SWCNT dispersion solution; subsequently, we prepared the p-type films via the drop-casting method. Sb2Te3 is a traditional p-type chalcogenide, which exhibits high thermoelectric performance near 300 K34–36, and Sb2Te3 nanoparticles were synthesized via a spontaneous redox reaction37. This method uses pitting corrosion, which is caused by the action of chloride ions on the substrate surface, as well as galvanic replacement, which is caused by the difference in the standard reduction potential between the materials. The p-type Sb2Te3 layers were formed on the nanocomposite films via the electrodeposi- tion method38. We tuned the quantity of Sb2Te3 nanoparticles in the SWCNT films to investigate the films with high thermoelectric performance. Experimental setup Figure 1 shows a schematic of the fabrication process of the SWCNT films containing Sb2Te3 nanoparticles and the coating of the Sb2Te3 electrodeposited layers. First, the nanoparticles were synthesized via the spontaneous redox reaction using an aluminum substrate (50 mm × 100 mm, 2 mm thick). Prior to nanoparticle synthesis, to remove any oxide layers from the aluminum substrate, it was placed in a 1 M NaOH (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Co.) solution for 5 min, followed by cleaning in deionized (DI) water (i.e., > 18 MΩ). The spontaneous redox reaction was conducted between the sacrificial aluminum plate and an electrolyte containing 0.02 M Sb2O3 (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory Co., Ltd.), 0.04 M TeO2 (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory Co., Ltd.), and 4.0 M HCl (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Co.) for 40 min at approximately 25 °C. After the reaction, the nanoparticles were washed with DI water, filtered, and dried under vacuum at 60 °C for 12 h. Figure 1. Scientific Reports | (2023) 13:5783 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-33022-4 2 Vol:.(1234567890)www.nature.com/scientificreports/ For film preparation, SWCNTs synthesized by the super-growth method (SG-CNTs) (ZEONANO SG101, ZEON Co.) were used as the starting material39. Powdered SG-CNTs (80 mg) were dispersed in 40 mL of etha- nol to prepare an SWCNT dispersion solution with a concentration of 0.25 wt%, and homogenized mixing was ensured using an ultrasonic homogenizer (SONICS 85, AZONE Co.). Next, the fabricated nanoparticles (5, 10, 50, and 100 mg) were added to the SWCNT dispersion solution, followed by mixing using the ultrasonic homogenizer. The nanocomposite films were prepared by a vacuum filtration method. A membrane filter (PTFE, 90 mm diameter: ADVANTEC) was placed in a filter holder in a suction bottle, and the dispersion solution was filtered by reducing the pressure in the suction bottle using a rotary pump. The entire volume of the nanoparticle- containing SWCNT-dispersion solution was poured dropwise onto the filter and aspirated for 1 h to produce the nanocomposite films with a diameter of 80 mm. After drying for air-drying 24 h, the nanocomposite films (thickness = 100 µm) were removed from the membrane filter. For electrodeposition, Sb2Te3 layers were prepared at approximately 25 °C by potentiostatic electrodeposition using a standard three-electrode cell. The electrolytes contained mixtures of 1.88 mM Sb2O3, 0.63 mM TeO2, and 0.58 M HCl diluted with DI water. The working electrode (electrode area: 7.8 cm2) was the nanocomposite film, which was fixed to a stainless-steel plate using polyimide tape. A platinum-coated titanium mesh on a titanium plate was used as the counter electrode (electrode area: 7.8 cm2). A Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode was used as the reference electrode. The electrode voltage was set at − 0.01 V using a potentiostat/galvanostat (HA-151B, Hokuto Denko) based on our previous report40, and electrodeposition was performed for 1 h. The precise structure of the nanoparticles was analyzed using high-resolution transmission electron micros- copy (HR-TEM, JEOL JEM-ARM200F), selected area electron diffraction (SAED), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) elemental mapping. The crystallographic properties of the nanoparticles and films were evaluated by X-ray diffraction (XRD; Mini Flex II, Rigaku) using Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm in the 2θ range from 20° to 70°). The microstructures of the films were analyzed with field emission scanning electron micros- copy (FE-SEM, Hitachi S-4800). The chemical compositions of the nanoparticles and nanocomposite films were determined with an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA, Shimadzu EPMA-1610). The compositions of the samples were calibrated using the ZAF4 program installed with the EPMA-1610. The in-plane electrical conductivity was measured at approximately 25 °C by a four-point probe method with an accuracy of ± 5%. The in-plane Seebeck coefficient of the nanocomposite films was measured at approximately 25 °C with an accuracy of ± 7%41. We used two K-type thermocouples of 0.1 mm in diameter, which were pressed on the center of the film. The distance between the thermocouples was 13 mm. One end of the film was connected to a heat sink and the other end to a heater. The Seebeck coefficient was determined as the ratio of the potential difference (ΔV) along the film to the temperature difference. The power factor was estimated from the measured electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient with an accuracy of ± 10%. Results and discussion Synthesis of the Sb2Te3 nanoparticles. The Sb2Te3 nanoparticles were synthesized via a spontaneous + and redox reaction, where an aluminum plate was immersed in a hydrochloric acid solution containing HTeO2 SbO+ ions. The difference in the redox potential for Al3+/Al0 (E0 = − 1.676 V vs. NHE) is more cathodic than for SbO+/Sb0 (E0 = + 0.212 V vs. NHE) and HTeO2 +/Te0 (E0 = + 0.353 V vs. NHE)42. The galvanic displacement of the aluminum plate to the Sb2Te3 nanoparticles can be represented as follows: 3HTeO+ Sb2Te0 2 (cid:31)aq(cid:30) + 2SbO+ 3(s) + 8H2O + 6Al3+ (cid:31)aq(cid:30) + 13H+ (cid:31)aq(cid:30) + 6Al0(s) → (1) Note that the direct formation of the Sb2Te3 intermetallic compound is thermodynamically favorable over the formation of Sb0 and Te0 because the Gibbs free energy of Sb2Te3 formation is negative (i.e. ΔGf 0 = − 57.5 kL/ mol)42. In Fig. 2a, the TEM micrograph shows that irregularly shaped particles with a size less than 100 nm are agglomerated. In Fig. 2b, the HR-TEM image of the near-surface of the nanoparticles shows that the nanoparticles exhibit a polycrystalline phase with grain boundaries of nanometer-sized single crystals, which corresponds to the SAED pattern in the inset. No lattice fringes are observed on the topmost surface of the particles (area A), indicating the formation of an amorphous layer. In Fig. 2c, the XRD pattern of the nanoparticles includes the peaks originating from Sb2Te3 and Te, corresponding to the SAED pattern in the inset of Fig. 2b. The elemental mapping and atomic composition of the nanoparticles are shown in Fig. 2d. In the elemental mapping, antimony and tellurium are almost uniformly distributed within the particles. The atomic percentages of antimony and tellurium are 33.1 and 66.9 at%, respectively. This atomic composition ratio deviates from the stoichiometric ratio (Sb/Te = 40/60) by approximately 7% towards the Te-rich side because of the presence of a Te crystalline phase in addition to the Sb2Te3 crystalline phase. For comparison, we synthesized Sb2Te3 nanoparticles via a spontaneous redox reaction using nickel and copper plates. The characteristics of the synthesized nanoparticles are provided in Supplementary Information (Fig. S1). As a result, the atomic compositions of the nanoparticles from the nickel and copper plates determined by EPMA significantly differ from the stoichiometric proportions: Sb/Te = 3.2/96.8 at% for the nickel plate and Sb/Te = 12.2/87.8 at% for the copper plate. This is because nickel and copper are less prone to pitting corrosion by chloride ions43,44, and thus the galvanic displacement reaction is not active. In Fig. 3f, there are no Sb2Te3 layers on the bundle surface of the film, even though electrodeposition was performed. Therefore, in the absence of nanoparticles within the films, it is difficult to form an electrodeposited layer on the films. At 5 mg nanoparticles (Fig. 3g), tiny spines appeared on the SWCNT bundle surface. The enlarged image in the inset shows that angular crystals sparsely grew on the surface. At 10 mg nanoparticle content, the size and density of the angular crystals increase (Fig. 3h). At 50 mg, the crystals further grow and completely cover the SWCNT bundle surface (Fig. 3i), while at 100 mg, the crystal shape changes to a fine flower-like structure (Fig. 3j), indicative of dendritic growth. The electrodeposition layers are formed not only on the surface of the SWCNT film, but also on the inside of the film. Table 1 shows the atomic compositions of the nanocomposite films with varying nanoparticle content after electrodeposition. Antimony and tellurium are not detected in the film without the nanoparticles. At a nanopar- ticle content of 5–100 mg, the atomic composition of the nanocomposite films is almost constant at Sb: 24 ± 1 at% and Te: 76 ± 1 at%, despite the large differences in crystal size and shape of the films. This is because the atomic composition of alloy films mainly depends on the applied voltage during electrodeposition45,46. Therefore, even though the atomic composition of the films deviated from the stoichiometric ratio (Sb: 40 at% and Te: 60 at%), an electrodeposition layer was formed on the surface of the SWCNT bundle by adding nanoparticles to the film. Further, the structure of the electrodeposited layer was tuned by changing the nanoparticle content. To evaluate the compositional homogeneity of the films, EDS maps are provided in Supplementary Information (Fig. S2). The EDS maps showed that antimony and tellurium were uniformly deposited on the surface of the SWCNTs and that the SWCNTs were less exposed. In addition, the XRD pattern of the typical nanocomposite film containing 10 mg of nanoparticles with electrodeposition is provided in Supplementary Information (Fig. S3). Here, we discuss the mechanism of crystal growth of the electrodeposited layers on the nanoparticle-contain- ing SWCNT films. In previous reports, Bi2Te3 crystals were grown on CNT surfaces via the sputtering process and solvothermal synthesis19,24. In addition, thin layers were electrodeposited on a SWCNT surface by tuning the surface condition of the SWCNT films29. These results suggest that layers of inorganic chalcogenides can grow on the CNT surface via electrodeposition under appropriate conditions. The key factors of electrodeposition are the ion concentration around the SWCNTs and current density47. The quantity of chemicals used during electrodeposition was the same in all the samples; however, the concentration of the precursor ions around the SWCNTs increases as the nanoparticle content in the film increases because the nanoparticles dissolve when exposed to dilute HCl. As a result, the current density increases as shown in Supplementary Information (Table S1). Therefore, in the case of the SWCNT film without nanoparticles, Sb2Te3 crystals do not grow because the densities of the Sb and Te nuclei are too low, and the crystals possibly re-melt before the crystal size reaches the critical nucleus radius48. In the presence of nanoparticles, the ion concentration around the SWCNTs and current density passing through the film increase and promote crystal growth. However, when the ion concen- tration and current density are too high, dendritic growth occurs47, as shown in Fig. 3j. Thermoelectric properties of nanocomposite films. Figure 4 shows the in-plane thermoelectric properties of the nanocomposite films as a function of nanoparticle content. In Fig. 4a, the electrical conductiv- ity of the normal SWCNT film (without nanoparticles and no electrodeposition) is 42 S/cm. As the nanoparticle content increases, the electrical conductivity of the nanocomposite film excluding electrodeposition slightly increases, indicating that the nanoparticles fill the gaps between the SWCNT bundles. The electrical conductiv- ity of the nanocomposite film with 100 mg nanoparticles is 78 S/cm, which is 86% higher than that of the normal SWCNT film. The increase in electrical conductivity is due to the nanoparticles between the SWCNT bundles serving to increase the current paths. On the other hand, by performing electrodeposition on the films contain- ing the nanoparticles, the electrical conductivity of the films is significantly affected by the quantity of nanopar- ticle. At 5 mg nanoparticle content and electrodeposition, the electrical conductivity is 179 S/cm, which is three times higher than that of the electrodeposited film without nanoparticles. At a higher nanoparticle content, the electrical conductivity further increases. At 100 mg, the electrical conductivity reaches 322 S/cm, which is 5.6 times higher than that of electrodeposited SWCNT film without nanoparticles. Therefore, the electrical con- ductivity is significantly increased by the increased thickness of the electrodeposited layer due to the increased quantity of nanoparticles. (a) Electrical conductivity, (b) Seebeck coefficient, and (c) power factor. In Fig. 4b, all films exhibit a p-type property due to the positive Seebeck coefficient. The Seebeck coefficient of the nanocomposite film excluding electrodeposition ranges from 55 to 60 µV/K and is independent of the nano- particle content. On the other hand, by performing electrodeposition on the films containing the nanoparticles, the Seebeck coefficient of the films decreases. At 5 mg nanoparticle content, the electrodeposited film exhibits a Seebeck coefficient of 40 µV/K, which approximately remains the same even at higher nanoparticle contents. The decrease in the Seebeck coefficient compared to the normal SWCNT films occurs because the electrodeposited Sb2Te3 layer exhibits a low Seebeck coefficient owing to the deviation from the stoichiometric proportion38. Since the deviation from the stoichiometric ratio is constant regardless of the quantity of nanoparticles, the Seebeck coefficient is largely constant, while there are differences in the thickness and surface morphology of the electrodeposited layers. In Fig. 4c, when the electrodeposition is not performed, the power factor slightly increases as the quantity of nanoparticles increases. The power factor of the nanocomposite film with 100 mg nanoparticles is 25.1 µW/ (m K2), which is two times higher than that of the normal SWCNT film. On the other hand, when electrodepo- sition is performed on films containing the nanoparticles, the power factor of the films greatly increases. In particular, at 100 mg nanoparticles with electrodeposition, the power factor is 59.5 µW/(m K2), which is 2.4 and 4.7 times higher than that of the corresponding nanocomposite film with no electrodeposition and the normal SWCNT film, respectively. Here, we compared the power factor in this study with that shown in the above- mentioned literature, where hybrid thin films of SWCNTs and Sb2Te3 nanoplates were prepared by vacuum filtration, followed by annealing20. Although no annealing was performed, the maximum power factor in this study (59.5 µW/(m K2)) was comparable to the maximum value in the literature (55 µW/(m K2)). Therefore, a significant improvement in the thermoelectric performance of Sb2Te3 nanoparticle-containing flexible SWCNT films subjected to Sb2Te3 layer electrodeposition is observed. To further improve the perfor- mance of the nanocomposite films, the Seebeck coefficient should be increased. A feasible approach is to optimize electrodeposition to form Sb2Te3 layers of stoichiometric proportion. In this study, the thermal conductivity of the nanocomposite films was not measured, and thus we calculated the thermal conductivity of the nanocomposite films based on the respective thermal conductivities of the SWCNT films, Sb2Te3 nanoparticles, and Sb2Te3 elec- trodeposited films. The calculated thermal conductivity is provided in Supplementary Information (Table S2). In the future, the calculated thermal conductivity should be verified by measuring the thermal conductivity of the nanocomposite films, and the thermoelectric properties should be analyzed in more detail. Conclusions Herein, the thermoelectric performance of the flexible SWCNT films was improved by containing the Sb2Te3 nanoparticles synthesized via spontaneous redox reaction in the SWCNT films, which was followed by the elec- trodeposition of the Sb2Te3 layer on the SWCNT bundle surface. When the nanoparticles were not contained in the SWCNT film, the Sb2Te3 layers were not formed using the electrodeposition. In contrast, the nanoparticles were contained in the SWCNT films, and the Sb2Te3 crystals were grown on the SWCNT bundle surface, even though the atomic composition of the electrodeposited layer deviated from the stoichiometric proportion. The crystal size and density of the electrodeposited Sb2Te3 increased with an increase in the quantity nanoparticles. Furthermore, increasing the concentration of precursor ions around SWCNTs via nanoparticle melting was the key to crystal growth, thus leading to the increase in the current density. The maximum power factor of the SWCNT films with Sb2Te3 electrodeposition was 59.5 µW/(m K2), which was 4.7 times higher than that of the normal SWCNT film. The proposed method can be extended to various other chalcogenide-SWCNT materials, thus demonstrating considerable potential for fabricating thermoelectric generators using both p- and n-type flexible thermoelectric films with excellent performance.
